domain.title: System Design in Practice
domain.tag: the interview · and the actual craft
domain.why: System design isn't a test of facts — it's a test of how you think when the problem is genuinely ambiguous and there's no single right answer. Most people fail at this not because they don't know enough, but because they describe one system from memory instead of actually reasoning about tradeoffs out loud and being willing to change their mind when new information shows up.

sections.t: How the interview is actually scored

L0.body:
The opening script. Say these out loud, in order, in the first eight minutes:

  FUNCTIONAL   what it must do   'post, follow, read a timeline. No DMs.'
  SCALE        DAU, req/user/day '100M DAU, 10 reads and 1 write each'
  SHAPE        read:write ratio  '10:1 read-heavy'
  LATENCY      target percentile 'p99 read under 200 ms, write 1 s'
  CONSISTENCY  per data class    'timeline eventual, follows RYW'
  AVAILABILITY target and cost   '99.9 percent, 43 min per 30 days'
  OUT OF SCOPE what you will not build

Then: 'Anything you want to change before I design to it?'
L0.cloze: Order: {{c1::functional}} requirements, then {{c2::scale}}, read:write {{c3::ratio}}, {{c4::latency}} target as a percentile, {{c5::consistency}} per data class, availability, and an explicit {{c6::out of scope}} list.

concepts.L1: Spend the first 5-10 minutes on scope. Functional requirements, then explicit non-functional ones: scale, latency targets, consistency needs, availability targets, read/write ratio.
concepts.L2: Candidates who start drawing boxes in minute two fail here regardless of what they draw. The interviewer's rubric almost always has an explicit 'clarified requirements' line, and it's the cheapest point in the loop.
concepts.L3: The requirements phase is not politeness, it is where you fix the free variables that every later number depends on. Without DAU you cannot derive QPS; without QPS you cannot size the fleet; without a read:write ratio you cannot choose between fan-out on write and fan-out on read; without a latency percentile you cannot decide whether a cross-region hop is allowed at all. A design built on unstated assumptions cannot be defended, because any pushback lands on a number you never committed to. State them out loud and the interviewer becomes a collaborator correcting inputs rather than an examiner hunting for gaps.

L4.prompt_tpl: You are told {D} million DAU and {R} requests per user per day, read:write {ratio} to 1. Derive average read QPS and average write QPS, and state the one further requirement you still need before you can pick a storage engine. Answer with the average read QPS.
L4.answer: total $= D \times 10^{6} \times R / 86400$; reads $=$ total $\times$ ratio/(ratio+1); writes $=$ total/(ratio+1). D=100,R=10,ratio=10: total 11574 rps, reads 10522, writes 1052. D=50,R=12,ratio=4: total 6944, reads 5556, writes 1389. D=200,R=20,ratio=100: total 46296, reads 45838, writes 458.
L4.explanation: 86400 seconds in a day is the only constant. The missing requirement is the latency target as a percentile: 1000 writes per second is trivial at p99 of 1 second and hard at p99 of 5 ms, and that single number decides synchronous versus queued writes.

L4.prompt_tpl: An interviewer says 'design a ride-hailing backend' and nothing else. Write the {n} clarifying questions you would ask, ordered by how much each one changes the architecture, and say what each answer would change.
L4.answer: Ordered by architectural leverage: (1) matching latency target, which decides in-memory geo index versus database; (2) geographic scope and data residency, which decides single-region versus multi-region; (3) write rate of driver location pings, which decides whether locations go to a database at all; (4) consistency requirement on the ride-accept step, which decides whether a distributed lock or a single-partition transaction is needed; (5) read:write ratio; (6) out-of-scope list.
L4.explanation: The ordering is the signal, not the list. Questions whose answers cannot change the diagram are filler. Ask the ones where each possible answer produces a visibly different design.

L0.body:
The four estimates, always in this order, always with units:

  QPS        DAU * req_per_user / 86400,      then * peak_factor
  STORAGE    events_per_day * bytes_per_event * retention_days * replication
  BANDWIDTH  QPS * payload_bytes            -> bytes/s -> bits/s
  MACHINES   QPS / per_machine_capacity,      then / target_utilisation

Worked: 100e6 * 10 / 86400 = 11574 rps average; peak factor 3 -> 34722 rps.
At 2 KiB per response: 34722 * 2048 = 71.1 MB/s = 0.57 Gbit/s.
At 2000 rps per machine and 0.5 target utilisation: 34722/2000/0.5 = 35 machines.
L0.cloze:
QPS = DAU * req_per_user / {{c1::86400}}, then multiply by the {{c2::peak}} factor.
Storage = events/day * bytes * retention * {{c3::replication}}.
Machines = peak QPS / per-machine capacity / {{c4::target utilisation}}.

concepts.L1: Derive QPS, storage growth, bandwidth, and machine count from stated assumptions. State the assumptions out loud so they can be corrected.
concepts.L2: The number matters less than showing the derivation. 100M DAU × 10 requests/day ÷ 86400 ≈ 12K QPS average, ×3 for peak ≈ 35K. That calculation, done out loud, is the signal.
concepts.L3: Every one of these is a unit conversion with one judgement call, and naming the judgement call is what reads as senior. 86400 is not a judgement. The peak factor is: traffic is not uniform over a day, so a 3x to 5x ratio of peak hour to daily mean is the usual band, and for an event-driven product like live sport it can be 50x. The target utilisation is the other one, and it is a queueing decision, not a budgeting one. Dividing by 0.5 rather than 0.9 doubles the fleet and is still correct, because at 0.9 utilisation an M/M/1 queue multiplies response time by ten. Do the arithmetic out loud, then name which two inputs are guesses.

L4.prompt_tpl: Peak load is {q} requests per second. One machine sustains {c} requests per second at saturation and you want to run at {u} percent utilisation with N plus one redundancy. How many machines do you provision? Answer with the number of machines provisioned.
L4.explanation: Two multipliers hide here and both are commonly dropped. Utilisation headroom is queueing, not waste. The plus one is so that losing a machine does not push the survivors past the utilisation target and trigger the latency cliff you just paid to avoid.

L4.prompt_tpl: A service stores {E} million events per day at {B} bytes each, keeps them for {d} days, and replicates {r} ways. Give bytes per day and total provisioned bytes. Answer with the total provisioned bytes.
L4.answer: per day $= E \times 10^{6} \times B$; total $= $ per day $\times d \times r$. E=500,B=200: 100 GB/day; d=365,r=3 gives 109.5 TB. E=1000,B=120: 120 GB/day; d=90,r=3 gives 32.4 TB. E=50,B=1500: 75 GB/day; d=30,r=2 gives 4.5 TB.
L4.explanation: Replication multiplies provisioned capacity and is the term candidates skip. Indexes and write amplification in an LSM store add more on top; a factor of 1.3 to 2 over raw bytes is a defensible allowance to state out loud.

L0.body:
The four-beat loop, repeated for every component:

  1 PROPOSE   'I'll shard the timeline store by user_id.'
  2 WHY       'Timeline reads are always keyed by one user, so this keeps them single-shard.'
  3 COST      'It makes global queries like trending scatter-gather across all shards.'
  4 CHECK     'I'll accept that and handle trending separately. Sound right, or push back?'

Then move. Never end a beat on silence waiting to be prompted.
L0.cloze: The loop is {{c1::propose}}, {{c2::why}}, {{c3::cost}}, {{c4::check in}} — then move on without waiting to be asked the next question.

concepts.L1: Propose a direction, state why, name the tradeoff, and check in. Do not wait to be asked. Senior signal is you owning the structure of the hour.
concepts.L2: The most common L6 downlevel reason is passivity — a technically fine design where the interviewer had to do the steering. Being right is necessary and not sufficient.
concepts.L3: The hour is a fixed budget and the interviewer is scoring how it gets spent. If they have to ask 'what about the database?' then they allocated that minute, not you, and the rubric line for leadership or ambiguity-handling reads as unmet regardless of your answer. The four-beat loop works because it makes every claim falsifiable in the same breath, which converts silence into a decision point they can either accept or redirect. It also protects you: an interviewer who redirects at beat four costs you thirty seconds, whereas one who redirects after you have drawn the whole design costs you fifteen minutes you will not get back.

L4.prompt_tpl: You are {m} minutes into a 45-minute round and have covered requirements and a high-level diagram. Write the exact sentence you use to take control of the next segment, and say which rubric line it targets.
L4.answer: Something of the form: 'The riskiest part here is timeline fan-out, so I want to spend the next ten minutes there and come back to search if we have time — unless you'd rather I go elsewhere.' It targets the leadership or ambiguity-handling line by naming a priority, a time budget, and an explicit offer to be overridden.
L4.explanation: Naming the time budget is what distinguishes driving from rambling. It shows you are managing a scarce resource, and it gives the interviewer a cheap way to redirect without derailing you.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two candidates produce the same architecture. Candidate A answers {n} interviewer questions correctly and volunteers nothing. Candidate B volunteers the same content unprompted and is wrong once. Predict the two scores and justify.
L4.answer: B usually scores higher. A's transcript shows the interviewer generating structure; the rubric reads that as needing direction. B's shows the candidate generating structure and self-correcting, which is what the senior bar measures. Being wrong once and recovering is itself positive evidence, provided the recovery is reasoned rather than capitulating.
L4.explanation: Interview rubrics score the process, not the artefact, because the artefact is not the job. This is the single most counterintuitive thing about the format and the most common downlevel reason at senior and above.

L0.body:
The sentence template, with the cost never optional:

  'I'll use <choice>, which buys <benefit> and costs <specific, named cost>.
   Is <cost> acceptable for <this data / this path>?'

Real instances:
  'Read replicas: cheap read scale, costs replication lag, so read-your-writes breaks.'
  'Async writes via queue: absorbs bursts, costs a window where the write is invisible.'
  'gRPC: smaller and faster, costs browser support and human-readable debugging.'
  'Multi-region active-active: survives a region, costs conflict resolution on every write.'
L0.cloze: Template: 'I'll use X, which buys {{c1::benefit}} and costs {{c2::a specific named cost}}. Is that acceptable for {{c3::this data class}}?'

concepts.L1: Every choice should come with what it costs. 'I'll use a cache here, which means accepting bounded staleness — is that acceptable for this data?'
concepts.L2: Unqualified recommendations read as inexperience. The senior habit is that no choice is stated without its cost, and interviewers listen for exactly this pattern.
concepts.L3: A recommendation without a cost is not a recommendation, it is a preference, and preferences are what juniors have. Every distributed-systems choice trades against one of a small set of resources: consistency, latency, availability, money, or operational complexity. If you cannot name which one you just spent, you did not know you were spending. The habit also pays off mid-interview: stating the cost yourself pre-empts the follow-up and converts a gap they found into a decision you made. The specific cost matters. 'It adds complexity' is a non-answer; 'it adds a second failure domain that must be drained before deploys' is a cost.

L4.prompt_tpl: A candidate says: 'I'll put a {ttl}-second TTL cache in front of the user profile service to reduce database load.' Identify what is missing from the statement and rewrite it correctly.
L4.answer: The cost is missing. Rewrite: 'A TTL cache in front of profiles cuts database reads by roughly the hit ratio, and costs up to one TTL of staleness after a profile edit, so a user who changes their display name may see the old one for that long. Acceptable for profiles; not for anything used in an authorisation decision.'
L4.explanation: Naming the exact staleness bound and the one data class where it is unacceptable is the difference between reciting a pattern and designing. Authorisation data is the standard counterexample.

L4.prompt_tpl: For each of these {n} choices name the single resource being spent: read replicas, an async write queue, synchronous cross-region replication, and a materialised view.
L4.answer: Read replicas spend consistency (replication lag). An async write queue spends visibility, a form of consistency, and adds an ordering and duplicate-delivery problem. Synchronous cross-region replication spends latency, bounded below by the speed of light. A materialised view spends write cost and freshness, plus the operational cost of rebuilding it.
L4.explanation: Everything in this domain trades against consistency, latency, availability, money, or operational complexity. Being able to say which one, per choice, in one word, is the fluency being tested.

L0.body:
Two scripts. Use whichever the evidence supports, never whichever is more comfortable.

  UPDATING
    'You're right — I was assuming reads dominate, and if writes are 50 percent
     then fan-out on write is wrong here. Let me redo that piece.'

  HOLDING
    'I want to keep this, and here's why: the failure you're describing needs
     both a region loss and a stale replica. We're at 99.9, and that joint
     event is well below the budget. What am I missing?'

Both end by handing the turn back. Neither ends in 'sure, whatever you prefer'.
L0.cloze: Updating names the {{c1::assumption}} that changed. Holding names the {{c2::reason}} and ends with {{c3::what am I missing}}. Neither is bare {{c4::capitulation}}.

concepts.L1: When the interviewer pushes back, evaluate the point genuinely. Update if they're right, hold with reasons if they're not.
concepts.L2: Interviewers frequently push back on correct answers to test this specifically. Both immediate capitulation and stubbornness score badly; reasoned engagement is what's being measured.
concepts.L3: Interviewers push back on correct answers precisely because the response separates two populations that look identical on a whiteboard. Someone who folds immediately will fold in a design review against a louder colleague, which is expensive. Someone who cannot be moved will ship the wrong thing, which is more expensive. The rubric wants evidence that new information updates a belief in proportion to its weight: identify which premise the objection attacks, decide whether it was load-bearing, and say so. If it was, redo the piece resting on it. If not, say which fact makes the objection non-binding, and invite the correction.

L4.prompt_tpl: You proposed eventual consistency for a feed. The interviewer says 'users will see posts out of order, that's unacceptable' when your target is p99 under {ms} ms. Decide whether to update or hold, and write the response.
L4.answer: Mostly hold, with a scoped concession: 'Out-of-order across authors is invisible to users because the feed is sorted by post timestamp on read, not arrival. What is visible is a user not seeing their own post, so I'll add read-your-writes for the author's own posts via a session-pinned read. The rest stays eventual.' That names the real failure mode inside the objection and fixes only that.
L4.explanation: Strong answers decompose an objection instead of accepting or rejecting it whole. Here the general claim is wrong and one special case inside it is right, and separating the two is the signal.

L4.prompt_tpl: Rank these {n} responses to interviewer pushback from strongest to weakest: immediate agreement and redesign; silent redesign; asking what failure they have in mind before responding; restating the original design louder.
L4.answer: Strongest: asking which failure they have in mind, because it costs ten seconds and makes the rest of the exchange evidence-based. Then immediate agreement with redesign, which is at least responsive. Then silent redesign, which loses the reasoning the rubric is scoring. Weakest: restating louder, which is non-responsive.
L4.explanation: A clarifying question is almost always the strongest first move under pushback: it is cheap, it is not capitulation, and it converts a vague objection into a specific one you can actually answer.

L0.body:
Depth checklist for the one component you pick. If you cannot fill all six, pick another.

  DATA MODEL  exact keys and index      'PK (user_id, post_id DESC)'
  SIZE        bytes/row, rows/shard     '250 B, 40M rows, 10 GB'
  HOT PATH    the query and its latency 'range scan 20 rows, p99 3 ms'
  FAILURE     what the client sees      'shard down -> 1/64 users 503'
  RECOVERY    who repairs it, how long  'replica promote, 30 s'
  NUMBERS     a figure nobody gave you  '10 GB per shard, so it fits in RAM'

Pick the component the requirements make riskiest, not the one you know best.
L0.cloze: Depth means naming the {{c1::data model}} with real keys, the bytes per row, the {{c2::hot path}} query with a latency, the {{c3::failure}} mode as the client sees it, recovery, and at least one {{c4::derived}} number.

concepts.L1: Breadth across the whole system, then pick one component and go all the way down — data model, failure modes, specific numbers.
concepts.L2: L6+ requires demonstrated depth somewhere. A design that stays uniformly at the box-and-arrow level reads as L4/L5 regardless of how complete it is.
concepts.L3: Breadth and depth are scored on different rubric lines and depth is the one that gates the senior bar, because breadth is memorisable and depth is not. A candidate who has read a system design book can draw a correct box diagram for any of thirty famous systems. Only someone who has operated something can say what the primary key is, what happens to the client when one shard is unavailable, and who gets paged. The checklist is a forcing function: each line is a question that has no answer unless you actually thought about this component. Choosing the riskiest component rather than the most familiar one is itself part of the signal, because it demonstrates you can identify risk.

L4.prompt_tpl: You chose to go deep on a timeline store holding {n} million rows across {s} shards at {b} bytes per row. Give bytes per shard, and state whether the working set fits in a {ram} GB page cache. Answer with the bytes per shard.
L4.answer: per shard $= n \times 10^{6} \times b / s$ bytes. n=2560,b=250,s=64: 10.0 GB per shard, fits in 64 GB with room for indexes. n=640,b=400,s=16: 16.0 GB, fits. n=10000,b=120,s=256: 4.69 GB, fits easily.
L4.explanation: The point of the arithmetic is the conclusion it licenses: once a shard fits in page cache the read path stops being a disk problem and becomes a network and serialisation problem, which changes what you optimise next. That inference chain is the depth signal.

L4.prompt_tpl: Given {s} shards and one shard fully unavailable, describe exactly what the client sees, what the error rate is, and what the repair is.
L4.answer: Users hash-mapped to that shard see errors; everyone else is unaffected. With uniform hashing the global error rate is 1/s: 1.56 percent at 64 shards, 6.25 percent at 16, 0.39 percent at 256. Repair is promoting a replica, tens of seconds, during which writes to that shard fail or queue. The uneven blast radius is the point: a small fraction of users see a total outage rather than everyone seeing a degraded service.
L4.explanation: Partial failure with an uneven blast radius is the normal shape of sharded outages, and being able to state the exact fraction and the recovery time is what separates operating experience from reading.

L0.body:
A typical senior-and-above rubric. Each line is scored independently.

  PROBLEM DEFINITION  scoped it, named targets, set out-of-scope
  ESTIMATION          derived numbers aloud, stated assumptions
  HIGH-LEVEL DESIGN   coherent components, storage justified
  DEPTH               one component to data model and failure modes
  TRADEOFFS           each choice paired with its cost
  OPERATIONS          deploy, migrate, observe, page
  COMMUNICATION       drove structure, handled pushback, kept time

Full marks on four lines and nothing on three is a downlevel.
L0.cloze: Rubric lines are scored {{c1::independently}}, so strength on one cannot compensate for a {{c2::blank}} on another. The two lines candidates most often leave empty are {{c3::operations}} and depth.

concepts.L1: System design rounds are scored against a fixed list of independent dimensions, not a single overall impression. Each line has its own evidence requirement, and a line with no evidence scores zero rather than averaging away.
concepts.L2: Strength does not transfer across lines. A candidate with a beautiful architecture and no operational discussion loses the operations line outright, and at senior level that alone can force a downlevel. Coverage across all seven beats brilliance on three.
concepts.L3: Rubrics are built this way to make the signal comparable across interviewers and to defend hiring decisions after the fact, which means the debrief is a per-line conversation and each interviewer must point at a moment in the transcript. That has a direct consequence for how you spend the hour: you need at least one concrete artefact per line, and the marginal value of a fourth clever remark on the same line is close to zero while the marginal value of the first sentence about migrations is large. Budget accordingly. Around minute thirty-five, if operations has not come up, raise it yourself in two sentences. The cheapest points in the entire loop are the lines nobody remembered to touch.

L4.prompt_tpl: With {m} minutes left and a complete high-level design but nothing said about deployment, migration or observability, choose between adding a caching tier and spending the time on operations. Justify against the rubric.
L4.answer: Spend it on operations. The caching tier adds evidence to a line already scored, likely at its ceiling; operations is currently zero. Two minutes each on expand-contract migration, canary plus feature flag, and RED metrics with an alert threshold converts a zero into a solid mark on a line that gates the senior bar.
L4.explanation: Marginal points, not total cleverness, is the right frame in a per-line rubric. This is the single highest-return habit in the format and almost nobody does it deliberately.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two candidates both score high on high-level design. One covers {a} of the seven lines and the other covers {b}. Explain why the debrief usually produces different levels rather than different scores.
L4.answer: Level is inferred from breadth of demonstrated responsibility, not peak quality. Missing lines read as things the candidate has never had to own: operations means never carried the pager, depth means never debugged their own design in production. Interviewers debate level, not score, and missing lines are what they have to argue about.
L4.explanation: This is why coverage beats brilliance. A missing line is read as absent experience rather than as an unlucky omission, because the interviewer has no evidence to argue otherwise.

concepts.t: The failure modes that downlevel you

L0.body:
Ranked by how often they appear in downlevel debriefs.

  1 PASSIVITY      the interviewer asked every question
  2 RECITATION     a known design, not derived from requirements
  3 NO NUMBERS     'it'll scale', with no QPS, bytes or machines
  4 UNIFORM DEPTH  every box at the same shallow level
  5 BARE CHOICES   'use Kafka' with no cost named
  6 NO OPS         no deploy, migration, alert or pager
  7 FOLDING        reversed a correct decision when questioned
  8 TIME BLOWOUT   twenty minutes on the API, nothing on storage

Seven of the eight are process failures, not knowledge failures.
L0.cloze: The most common downlevel reason is {{c1::passivity}}. The second is {{c2::recitation}} of a known architecture rather than deriving one. Only {{c3::one}} of the eight is a knowledge gap.

concepts.L1: The dominant reasons candidates get downlevelled in system design are behavioural, not technical: passivity, reciting a memorised architecture, omitting numbers, uniform shallow depth, and running out of time on a low-value section.
concepts.L2: Studying more systems fixes almost none of these. Recitation in particular gets worse with more study, because a larger library of memorised designs makes it easier to pattern-match the prompt to a stored answer instead of deriving one from the stated requirements.
concepts.L3: Consider why recitation is penalised even when the recited design is correct. The interviewer is trying to predict performance on a problem nobody has published an answer to, which is what the job actually is. A recited design provides no evidence about that, and it is detectable: the reciter's design does not change when the requirements do. The standard probe is to alter one requirement mid-round, making it write-heavy or adding a residency constraint, and watch whether the architecture moves. Someone deriving changes two components and explains why. Someone reciting keeps the diagram and adds a box.

L4.prompt_tpl: A candidate produces a correct architecture in {m} minutes flat, then waits. The interviewer changes one requirement from read-heavy to write-heavy and the candidate adds a queue and keeps everything else. Name the two failure modes and the probe that exposed them.
L4.answer: Passivity, shown by waiting after finishing, and recitation, shown by the design not moving when its premise did. A genuine read-heavy-to-write-heavy switch should change the storage engine argument toward LSM, revisit fan-out on write versus read, and change the sharding key discussion. Adding a queue is a bolt-on. The probe is the requirement flip, and it is deliberate.
L4.explanation: Requirement flips are the standard test for derivation versus recall. Expect one, and when it comes, say out loud which earlier decisions it invalidates before you redraw anything.

L4.prompt_tpl: You have used {m} of 45 minutes and are still on the API schema. Choose your next move and justify it against the ranked failure modes.
L4.answer: Cut the schema immediately and say so: 'I'll stop here on the API, the interesting risk is storage and fan-out, let me move.' This directly avoids time blowout and demonstrates the time management the communication line scores. Finishing the schema optimises a low-value line while guaranteeing zeros on depth and operations.
L4.explanation: Announcing the cut is worth as much as making it. It converts an implicit time-management failure into an explicit prioritisation decision, which is what the rubric rewards.

Ordered, with each step's ratio to the one above it:

  L1 cache reference               1 ns
  L2 cache reference               4 ns        4x
  main memory reference          100 ns       25x
  SSD random read                100 us     1000x
  same-datacenter round trip     500 us        5x
  HDD seek                        10 ms       20x
  cross-country round trip        40 ms        4x
  cross-Atlantic round trip       80 ms        2x
  Mumbai to US East round trip   200 ms      2.5x

Nine numbers spanning 1 ns to 200 ms: a factor of 200 million.

concepts.L1: L1 ~1ns, L2 ~4ns, main memory ~100ns, SSD random read ~100μs, HDD seek ~10ms, same-datacenter RTT ~0.5ms, cross-country ~40ms, cross-Atlantic ~80ms, India to US ~200ms.
concepts.L2: Speed of light in fiber is ~200,000 km/s, so Mumbai to Virginia is ~130ms round trip minimum, physically. No engineering removes that, and being able to state it settles a whole class of architecture arguments.
concepts.L3: Learn the ratios, not the absolute values, because the ratios license the design conclusions and they barely move across a decade of hardware. Memory to SSD is about 1000x, which is why a 99 percent cache hit ratio still leaves the miss term dominating mean latency. Same-datacenter to cross-country is about 80x, which is why a chatty protocol that is fine within a rack is fatal across regions: ten sequential round trips cost 5 ms locally and 400 ms across a continent. Absolute numbers drift, but network round trips have barely moved at all, because they are bounded by distance rather than by manufacturing.

L4.prompt_tpl: A request path makes {n} sequential dependent calls. Compute total added latency if each call is a same-datacenter round trip at 0.5 ms, and if each is cross-country at 40 ms. Answer with the cross-country total in milliseconds.
L4.answer: local $= 0.5n$ ms; remote $= 40n$ ms. n=4: 2 ms vs 160 ms. n=10: 5 ms vs 400 ms. n=25: 12.5 ms vs 1000 ms.
L4.explanation: Sequential dependent calls multiply the round trip, so chattiness is a latency bug that only appears once a component moves across a region boundary. This is the argument for batching and for coarse-grained APIs at region edges.

L4.prompt_tpl: Using memory at 100 ns and SSD random read at 100 us, compute the mean lookup time at a {h} percent cache hit ratio and the fraction of it contributed by misses. Answer with the mean lookup time in nanoseconds.
L4.answer: $T = h \cdot 100\,\text{ns} + (1-h) \cdot 100000\,\text{ns}$. h=0.95: 5095 ns, misses 98.1 percent. h=0.99: 1099.9 ns, misses 90.9 percent. h=0.999: 199.9 ns, misses 50.0 percent.
L4.explanation: With a 1000x gap the miss term dominates until the hit ratio passes about 99.9 percent. This is why chasing the last fraction of a percent of hit ratio is often the highest-value cache work, and why average latency is a misleading target.

L0.body:
Per-device ceilings, and what saturates first:

  NVMe SSD        ~1M IOPS,  3-7 GB/s
  10 GbE NIC      1.25 GB/s        (10 Gbit/s / 8)
  25 GbE NIC      3.125 GB/s
  DDR5 channel    ~50 GB/s
  NVLink 4        900 GB/s
  one CPU core    a few 10^9 simple ops/s

Conversion that gets dropped: Gbit/s / 8 = GB/s. A 10 GbE link moves
1.25 GB/s, which is one 7 GB/s NVMe drive running at 18 percent.
L0.cloze: 10 GbE is {{c1::1.25}} GB/s because bits divide by {{c2::8}}. DDR5 is about {{c3::50}} GB/s per channel, roughly {{c4::40}} times a 10 GbE link.

concepts.L1: Modern NVMe: ~1M IOPS, 3-7 GB/s. 10GbE: ~1.25 GB/s. DDR5: ~50 GB/s per channel. NVLink 4: 900 GB/s. A single core: a few billion simple ops/sec.
concepts.L2: Network is usually the binding constraint in distributed systems and memory bandwidth in single-machine ones. Knowing which resource you're actually saturating is most of performance work.
concepts.L3: The practical use is finding the binding constraint by dividing the offered load by each ceiling and seeing which quotient reaches one first. Take a service serving 200000 responses per second at 8 KiB each: that is 1.64 GB/s, which already exceeds a 10 GbE NIC at 1.25 GB/s while sitting at 3 percent of DDR5 bandwidth and well inside NVMe throughput. The answer is not a faster database, it is a bigger NIC or smaller responses. The general shape holds: in distributed systems the network is usually the first ceiling reached, and on a single machine it is usually memory bandwidth, because compute per byte in typical serving code is low. Always divide before you optimise.

L4.prompt_tpl: A service returns {q} responses per second averaging {b} KiB. Compute required egress in GB/s and Gbit/s, and state whether a 10 GbE NIC suffices. Answer with the required egress in Gbit/s.
L4.answer: bytes/s $= q \times b \times 1024$; Gbit/s $=$ bytes/s $\times 8 / 10^{9}$. q=200000,b=8: 1.638 GB/s = 13.1 Gbit/s, exceeds 10 GbE. q=50000,b=2: 0.102 GB/s = 0.82 Gbit/s, fine. q=20000,b=64: 1.311 GB/s = 10.5 Gbit/s, exceeds 10 GbE.
L4.explanation: The factor of 8 between bits and bytes is where this goes wrong most often. Note that the third case saturates a NIC at only 20000 requests per second, because payload size matters as much as request rate.

L4.prompt_tpl: A single-machine job reads {g} GB from page cache and does about {f} floating point operations per byte. Identify whether it is memory-bandwidth bound or compute bound and give the reasoning.
L4.answer: Compare arithmetic intensity against the machine ratio. A core doing a few times $10^{9}$ operations per second against roughly 50 GB/s of DDR5 needs about 0.1 operations per byte to keep up per core; a modern many-core socket needs on the order of 10 to 50. At 0.5 and 2 operations per byte the job is memory-bandwidth bound; at 20 it is closer to compute bound on a small core count and still bandwidth bound on a large one.
L4.explanation: This is the roofline argument in one line: arithmetic intensity versus the machine's operations-per-byte ratio. Which side you are on decides whether vectorising or reducing data movement is the win.

L0.body:
UUID                        16 B
  int64 timestamp              8 B
  typical database row     100-1000 B
  compressed JPEG          ~200 KB
  one minute of 1080p H.264 ~50 MB
  one FP16 parameter           2 B
  one FP8 parameter            1 B

The chain that matters:

  70e9 params * 1 B  =  70 GB   -> fits, with 10 GB left for KV cache
  8e9  params * 2 B  =  16 GB   -> fits on a 24 GB consumer card

concepts.L1: UUID 16 bytes, timestamp 8, a typical row 100-1000 bytes, a compressed image ~200KB, a minute of 1080p video ~50MB, an FP16 parameter 2 bytes.
concepts.L2: The last one lets you size models instantly: 70B parameters at FP16 is 140GB, so it doesn't fit on one 80GB H100, which immediately implies tensor parallelism. That inference chain is exactly the kind of thing that reads as fluency.
concepts.L3: Sizes are useful because they turn a vague question into a comparison against a fixed physical capacity, usually a well-known constant: 80 GB per H100, 24 GB per consumer GPU, 8 KiB per database page. The model chain is the highest-value instance. 70 billion FP16 parameters is 140 GB, which exceeds 80 GB, so one H100 is impossible and you need two GPUs with tensor parallelism or 8-bit quantisation to 70 GB. That leaves 10 GB for KV cache, and at 80 layers, 8 KV heads and head dimension 128 in FP16 the cache is 0.33 MB per token, so 10 GB holds about 30000 tokens of batch context. That is the real concurrency limit, from two multiplications.

L4.prompt_tpl: A model has {p} billion parameters. Give weight memory in GB at FP16 and at INT8, and the minimum number of {gmem} GB GPUs needed for FP16 weights alone. Answer with the number of GPUs needed for the FP16 weights.
L4.answer: FP16 $= 2p$ GB; INT8 $= p$ GB; GPUs $= \lceil 2p/\text{mem} \rceil$. p=70,mem=80: 140 GB, 70 GB, 2 GPUs. p=8,mem=24: 16 GB, 8 GB, 1 GPU. p=405,mem=80: 810 GB, 405 GB, 11 GPUs.
L4.explanation: Weights alone are a floor, not the requirement. Activations, KV cache and fragmentation typically need 20 to 40 percent more, so the honest answer adds a GPU beyond the ceiling division in the tight cases.

L4.prompt_tpl: A video service ingests {h} hours of 1080p per day at 50 MB per minute and keeps three transcode ladders totalling {ladder}x the original bytes. Give daily and annual storage. Answer with the daily storage in MB.
L4.answer: daily $= h \times 60 \times 50\,\text{MB} \times \text{mult}$. h=1000,mult=1.8: 5.4 TB/day, 1.97 PB/year. h=10000,mult=2.5: 75 TB/day, 27.4 PB/year. h=250,mult=1.8: 1.35 TB/day, 0.49 PB/year.
L4.explanation: Transcode ladders are the multiplier candidates forget: you store the source plus every rendition. At petabyte scale the storage bill is real but the egress bill on the same content is usually larger.

Order-of-magnitude cloud prices, USD, on-demand list:

  object storage        0.023 per GB-month
  internet egress       0.09  per GB          <- the expensive one
  H100 GPU              2-4   per hour
  general-purpose vCPU  25    per month
  managed NAT gateway   0.045 per GB processed

Serving that same 1 TB out once: 1024 * 0.09 = 92.16 USD.
Egress is roughly 4x the cost of storing the same bytes for a month.

concepts.L1: S3-class storage ~$0.023/GB/month. Egress ~$0.09/GB — the expensive one. An H100 ~$2-4/hour on demand. A c-class VM core ~$25/month.
concepts.L2: Egress cost dominates architecture for anything media-heavy. At Hotstar scale, CDN egress is the single largest infrastructure line item, and designs that ignore it are not credible.
concepts.L3: Egress dominates because it is charged per byte delivered while storage is charged per byte held, so the ratio between them is the access frequency. Storing a 200 KB image costs 0.0000046 USD per month; serving it once costs 0.000018 USD. At four views per month the bill flips, and at four hundred views egress is a hundred times storage. That ratio drives the entire CDN argument: a CDN is not primarily a latency optimisation, it is an egress arbitrage, since origin-to-CDN transfer is usually discounted and CDN-to-user is cheaper per GB than cloud egress.

L4.prompt_tpl: A service serves {v} million images per month at {kb} KB each. Compute monthly egress in TB and monthly egress cost at 0.09 USD per GB. Answer with the monthly egress cost in USD.
L4.explanation: Egress at scale is a headline line item, not a rounding error. Halving image size halves this bill directly, which is why format and quality decisions are cost decisions and belong in a design discussion.

L4.prompt_tpl: An object is {kb} KB and is viewed {n} times per month. Derive the view count at which monthly egress cost equals monthly storage cost at 0.023 USD per GB-month and 0.09 USD per GB egress. Answer with the breakeven view count.
L4.answer: Breakeven is where $n \times 0.09 = 0.023$, so $n = 0.023/0.09 = 0.256$ views per month, independent of object size. At any $n \geq 1$ egress already dominates: at n=1 by 3.9x, at n=10 by 39x, at n=1000 by 3913x.
L4.explanation: Size cancels, which is the surprising part. For anything served even once a month, egress is the dominant cost, so cold archival is the only regime where storage price matters more than delivery price.

concepts.t: QPS from DAU, in one line

L0.body:
QPS_avg  = DAU * requests_per_user_per_day / 86400
  QPS_peak = QPS_avg * peak_factor

Worked, 100M DAU at 10 requests per user per day:
  100e6 * 10 = 1e9 requests/day
  1e9 / 86400 = 11574 requests/second average
  * 3 = 34722 peak;  * 5 = 57870 peak

Reference points for the peak factor:
  global consumer product, no events        2-3x
  single-timezone product                   4-6x
  scheduled event (match start, sale open)  20-50x for minutes
L0.cloze: QPS average is DAU times requests per user divided by {{c1::86400}}. Multiply by a {{c2::peak factor}} of about 3 for a global product and up to {{c3::50}} for a scheduled event.

concepts.L1: The single most-used derivation in the format: daily active users times requests per user per day, divided by 86400 seconds, then multiplied by a peak factor. Every fleet-size and bandwidth number downstream depends on it.
concepts.L2: The peak factor is not a safety margin, it is a distributional fact, and picking it is where judgement lives. Provisioning for the daily mean means running at roughly 300 percent utilisation during peak hour, which is not slow, it is down.
concepts.L3: Traffic follows a diurnal curve, so the peak-hour rate is always above the daily mean and the ratio depends on how concentrated the user base is in time. A globally distributed product smears the curve and lands near 2 to 3; a product whose users are all in one timezone peaks harder, around 4 to 6. Scheduled events break the model entirely because the onset is seconds rather than hours, which is the case autoscaling cannot serve. Note also that the formula gives an average over the peak hour, not the instantaneous maximum: within that hour there is a further burst factor, so a second multiplier of 1.5 to 2 for the burstiest minute is defensible if you are sizing a queue rather than a fleet.

L4.prompt_tpl: A product has {D} million DAU and each user makes {r} requests per day. Give average QPS and peak QPS at a peak factor of {pf}. Answer with the peak QPS.
L4.explanation: Note the first and third cases: 100M users at 10 requests and 1B users at 3 requests differ by 3x, so the product of the two inputs is what matters and either alone tells you nothing.

L4.prompt_tpl: You provision for average QPS instead of peak. At a peak factor of {pf} and a per-machine saturation point of {c} requests per second, derive the utilisation your fleet reaches at peak and say what the user sees. Answer with the utilisation at peak as a percentage of capacity.
L4.answer: Utilisation at peak $=$ pf, expressed as a fraction of capacity: pf=3 gives 300 percent, pf=5 gives 500 percent, pf=2 gives 200 percent. The per-machine number cancels because the fleet was sized to exactly meet the mean. Above 100 percent the queue grows without bound, so users see latency climbing until timeouts, then errors.
L4.explanation: Offered load above service capacity is not slowness, it is an unbounded queue. Latency rises linearly with time until something sheds load or the process runs out of memory. This is why the peak factor is not optional.

L0.body:
raw_per_day = events_per_day * bytes_per_event
  provisioned = raw_per_day * retention_days * replication * overhead

Worked: 500M events/day at 200 B, 365-day retention, 3 replicas:
  500e6 * 200        = 1.0e11 B/day = 100 GB/day
  100 GB * 365       = 36.5 TB raw
  36.5 TB * 3        = 109.5 TB provisioned
  * 1.4 index/WAL    = 153.3 TB actual

Sanity check upward: 100 GB/day is 1.16 MB/s written. Trivial for one
NVMe drive. The problem is the year of retention, not the write rate.
L0.cloze: Provisioned bytes = events/day * bytes/event * {{c1::retention days}} * {{c2::replication}} * overhead. At 500M events/day of 200 B, that is {{c3::100}} GB/day and {{c4::109.5}} TB at 365 days with 3 replicas.

concepts.L1: Storage sizing is a four-factor product: event rate, bytes per event, retention window, and replication, with an overhead factor for indexes and write-ahead logs on top.
concepts.L2: Retention is usually the dominant term and it is usually a policy decision, not a technical one, so it is the cheapest thing to negotiate. Halving retention halves the bill instantly, while halving bytes per event takes a schema migration.
concepts.L3: The instructive part is that write rate and storage volume are almost unrelated problems. 500 million events per day is 5787 writes per second, which one well-tuned node handles; the same workload accumulates 109.5 TB of provisioned data in a year, which no single node holds. The design pressure comes from volume and query pattern, not ingestion, so the right response is tiering rather than sharding: the last seven days is 2.1 TB replicated and fits on one machine's SSDs, while the remaining 107 TB goes to object storage at about 2470 USD per month. Always compute both numbers, because they point at different solutions.

L4.prompt_tpl: A system logs {E} million events per day at {B} bytes, retains {d} days, replicates {r} ways, and has a {ov} overhead factor for indexes. Give provisioned TB and the sustained write rate in MB/s. Answer with the provisioned TB.
L4.explanation: Compare the two columns. All three cases are trivial write rates and non-trivial volumes, which is the normal shape of a logging or telemetry workload and the reason the answer is tiered storage rather than a bigger database.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need to cut a {tb} TB storage bill by half. Rank these levers by effort-to-saving: shorter retention, fewer replicas, compression, smaller schema, cold tiering.
L4.answer: Shortest path first: cold tiering, which is a config change and moves 90 percent of bytes to storage costing roughly a quarter as much, with no data loss. Then retention, a policy conversation with legal rather than an engineering project. Then compression, a one-time cost with a 2x to 5x return on text. Then schema shrinkage, which needs a migration. Fewer replicas last, because it trades durability and read capacity for money.
L4.explanation: Ranking by effort-to-saving rather than by saving alone is the senior move. Replica reduction has the cleanest arithmetic and the worst risk profile, which is exactly why it is the one to name last.

L0.body:
bytes_per_second = QPS * payload_bytes
  bits_per_second  = bytes_per_second * 8
  monthly_GB       = bytes_per_second * 2.592e6 / 1e9      (30 days)
  monthly_USD      = monthly_GB * 0.09                      (internet egress)

Worked, 34722 rps at 2 KiB:
  34722 * 2048     = 71.1 MB/s
  * 8              = 569 Mbit/s      (fits one 10 GbE link at 5.7 percent)
  * 2.592e6 / 1e9  = 184300 GB/month = 184.3 TB
  * 0.09           = 16587 USD/month

Same rate, 20 KiB payloads: 5.69 Gbit/s and 165870 USD/month.
L0.cloze: Bandwidth is QPS times payload bytes. Multiply by {{c1::8}} for bits. A month is about {{c2::2.592e6}} seconds. Internet egress at 0.09 USD/GB makes 71 MB/s cost about {{c3::16587}} USD per month.

concepts.L1: Bandwidth is the product of request rate and payload size, and it produces two independent constraints: a link-capacity constraint measured in bits per second, and a cost constraint measured in dollars per month.
concepts.L2: The two constraints bind at wildly different scales. A payload increase that is invisible against NIC capacity can be catastrophic against the egress bill, because links are provisioned in large discrete steps while egress is charged linearly per byte.
concepts.L3: Work the same load two ways. At 34722 requests per second and 2 KiB responses you need 569 Mbit/s, which is 5.7 percent of a single 10 GbE link, so capacity is a non-issue and you would never think about it again. The same figure is 184 TB per month, which at 0.09 USD per GB is 16587 USD per month of pure egress. Grow the payload to 20 KiB and capacity is still fine at 5.7 Gbit/s, while the bill becomes 165870 USD per month. So payload size is primarily a finance decision, and the levers are compression, field selection so clients do not fetch what they discard, and a CDN, which converts expensive origin egress into cheaper cached delivery at whatever the cache hit ratio turns out to be.

L4.prompt_tpl: A service runs at {q} requests per second with {kb} KiB responses. Give Gbit/s, monthly TB over 30 days, and monthly egress cost at 0.09 USD per GB. Answer with the monthly egress cost in USD.
L4.explanation: The last two cases are identical in every derived quantity because the product of rate and size is the same. Bandwidth and its bill do not care how you split the product, which is the whole point of computing it.

L4.prompt_tpl: A CDN in front of the origin achieves a {h} percent hit ratio. Origin egress is 0.09 USD per GB and CDN delivery is {cdn} USD per GB. Derive the total cost per GB delivered and the saving versus origin-only. Answer with the total cost per GB delivered.
L4.answer: cost per GB $= cdn + (1-h) \times 0.09$. h=0.90,cdn=0.02: 0.029, a 67.8 percent saving. h=0.95,cdn=0.02: 0.0245, 72.8 percent. h=0.99,cdn=0.04: 0.0409, 54.6 percent.
L4.explanation: Every byte still pays CDN delivery, so the CDN rate is a floor the hit ratio cannot beat. Case three shows a better hit ratio on a pricier CDN losing to case one, which is why the comparison must be done on the full expression rather than on hit ratio alone.

L0.body:
writes_to_storage = source_writes * average_fanout

Timeline fan-out on write, 1052 posts/second, mean 200 followers:
  1052 * 200 = 210400 timeline inserts/second

Now the tail of the follower distribution:
  a 50,000,000-follower account posting once
  = 50e6 inserts for one write
  at 210400 inserts/s of spare capacity, that is 238 seconds of the
  entire fleet's write budget, for one post

Hybrid cut-off: fan out on write below F followers, merge at read above it.
L0.cloze: Fan-out on write multiplies storage writes by the {{c1::average}} follower count, but the fleet is sized by the {{c2::tail}}: one 50M-follower post is {{c3::50 million}} inserts, which is why production systems use a {{c4::hybrid}} cut-off.

concepts.L1: Any fan-out design multiplies the write rate by the fan-out factor. The arithmetic is trivial; the trap is that the mean fan-out sizes the steady state while the maximum fan-out sizes the incident.
concepts.L2: Follower counts are heavy-tailed, so the mean is not a summary of anything. A system provisioned at 200x mean amplification is correctly sized for 99.99 percent of posts and catastrophically undersized for the 0.01 percent that determine whether the site stays up.
concepts.L3: Take 1052 posts per second and a mean of 200 followers: 210400 inserts per second, a large but ordinary write workload. Now add one account with 50 million followers. A single post from it demands 50 million inserts, which at the fleet's full 210400 per second takes 238 seconds. In practice the writes spread across shards, so it is not a total stall but a multi-minute latency excursion on every shard at once, which is worse to debug. The fix is a cut-off: accounts below a follower threshold fan out on write and get fast reads; accounts above it are merged at read time, costing a few extra reads per timeline load.

L4.prompt_tpl: A social product does {w} posts per second with mean fan-out {f}. Compute steady-state inserts per second, and the time to fan out one post from an account with {c} million followers if the whole fleet is dedicated to it. Answer with the steady-state inserts per second.
L4.answer: steady $= w \times f$; time $= c \times 10^{6} / (w \times f)$ seconds. w=1052,f=200,c=50: 210400 inserts/s, 237.6 s. w=500,f=50,c=10: 25000 inserts/s, 400 s. w=5000,f=800,c=100: 4000000 inserts/s, 25 s.
L4.explanation: Notice the third case: a fleet already provisioned for 4 million inserts per second absorbs a 100 million follower fan-out in 25 seconds. Tail fan-out hurts in proportion to how small your steady-state capacity is, which is why small products feel it worse.

L4.prompt_tpl: Set the hybrid cut-off. Fan-out on write costs 1 insert per follower. Read-time merge costs 1 extra read per followed celebrity per timeline load, and each user loads their timeline {L} times per day while a celebrity posts {P} times per day. Derive the follower count above which read-time merge is cheaper.
L4.answer: Write cost per celebrity post $= F$ inserts. Read cost per day $= F \times L$ extra reads for $P$ posts, so per post it is $F L / P$ reads. Read-merge wins when $F L / P < F$, i.e. when $L < P$, independent of $F$. So the cut-off is not a follower count at all: it depends on whether a celebrity posts more often than followers read. L=10,P=5: fan-out on write wins. L=4,P=1: write wins. L=30,P=20: write wins.
L4.explanation: The clean result is that $F$ cancels, so the naive framing is wrong: the real driver is the ratio of read frequency to post frequency, plus the fact that a single huge fan-out is a latency spike while merges are spread out. Production cut-offs are chosen for spike avoidance, not total work.

concepts.t: Geographic latency from the speed of light
