c in vacuum        299792 km/s
  c in fibre         c * 2/3 = 199862 km/s      (refractive index ~1.5)
  RTT_ideal          2 * distance / 199862 * 1000 ms
  RTT_real           RTT_ideal * 1.3 to 1.6     (routing is not great-circle)

  Mumbai  - N. Virginia   13000 km -> 130.1 ms ideal -> ~182 ms real
  London  - New York       5570 km ->  55.7 ms ideal ->  ~78 ms real
  SF      - New York       4130 km ->  41.3 ms ideal ->  ~58 ms real
  Mumbai  - Singapore      3900 km ->  39.0 ms ideal ->  ~55 ms real

No engineering removes the ideal term. It is a distance measurement.
L0.cloze: Light in fibre travels about {{c1::200000}} km/s because the refractive index is about {{c2::1.5}}. Round trip is {{c3::2}} times distance over that, and real routes add a factor of about {{c4::1.4}} for non-great-circle paths.

concepts.L1: Cross-region latency has a hard floor set by physics: light in glass travels at about two thirds of its vacuum speed, so a round trip costs at least twice the distance divided by 199862 km per second.
concepts.L2: The refractive index factor is the part people omit, and it is a third of the answer. Quoting a vacuum figure understates real fibre latency by 50 percent, which is the difference between a design that fits a 100 ms budget and one that does not.
concepts.L3: The derivation is one division and it settles arguments. Mumbai to Northern Virginia is roughly 13000 km great-circle. In vacuum that round trip would be 86.7 ms; in fibre at 199862 km/s it is 130.1 ms; and since cables follow coastlines rather than great circles, a factor of 1.3 to 1.6 gives 170 to 208 ms, which matches what you measure. The consequence is architectural: a synchronous write acknowledged in Virginia cannot serve a Mumbai user inside a 150 ms p99 budget however fast the database is, so you either place a write-capable replica in Asia, accept asynchronous replication, or move the target.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two datacentres are {d} km apart great-circle. Compute the ideal fibre round trip in ms and the realistic figure at a route factor of {rf}. Answer with the realistic round trip in milliseconds.
L4.explanation: 199862 km/s is 299792 times two thirds. The route factor is the only judgement in the calculation and stating your assumed value out loud is part of doing it properly.

L4.prompt_tpl: A p99 read budget of {ms} ms must be met for users in Mumbai against a primary in Northern Virginia. State whether it is physically possible and give the three architectural options.
L4.answer: At 150 and 100 ms it is impossible for a synchronous cross-region read: the floor is about 182 ms of network alone, before any server time. At 400 ms it is possible but leaves only about 218 ms of budget. The options are a read replica in Mumbai with eventual consistency, a regional cache with a stated staleness bound, or renegotiating the target. Saying 'impossible, here is the number' is stronger than proposing an optimisation.
L4.explanation: Physical impossibility is the cleanest form of a design argument and one of the few places where the correct answer is to reject the requirement rather than satisfy it.

concepts.t: Latency numbers you derive rather than recall

L0.body:
Derive, do not memorise. Two inputs give the whole table.

  time = size / bandwidth  +  fixed_access_latency

  1 MiB from DDR5 at 50 GB/s      1.049e6/50e9   =  21 us
  1 MiB from NVMe at 3 GB/s       1.049e6/3e9    = 350 us
  1 MiB over 10 GbE at 1.25 GB/s  1.049e6/1.25e9 = 839 us
  1 MiB over 1 GbE at 125 MB/s    1.049e6/125e6  = 8.4 ms

Compression, gzip decompressing at ~150 MB/s:
  1 MiB at 3:1 over 1 GbE: 2.8 transfer + 7.0 decompress = 9.8 ms
  1 MiB uncompressed over 1 GbE: 8.4 ms. Compression loses.
  Over a 10 MB/s WAN link it wins by about 70 ms.
L0.cloze: Transfer time is {{c1::size divided by bandwidth}} plus a fixed access latency. Compression pays off only when the {{c2::link}} is slower than the decompressor, which is why it wins on the {{c3::WAN}} and often loses inside a datacentre.

concepts.L1: Most latency figures worth knowing are a division: bytes divided by a bandwidth, plus a fixed access cost. Deriving them means you can answer for any size and any device rather than only the sizes someone tabulated.
concepts.L2: Memorised tables silently encode a size. 'Read 1 MB sequentially from memory: 250 microseconds' was true at 4 GB/s and is wrong by an order of magnitude on DDR5 at 50 GB/s. The division survives hardware changes; the table does not.
concepts.L3: The reason to hold bandwidths rather than durations is that bandwidth has improved roughly 10x per decade while access latency has improved perhaps 2x, so any memorised duration decays at a rate depending on which term dominated when it was written. Working from the division also makes crossover questions answerable. Compression is the clearest: it is worth doing exactly when the bytes saved cost more to transfer than the CPU costs to decompress, so the threshold is where link bandwidth falls below decompression throughput. At 150 MB/s that means compression loses on any faster link, which is why it is always on over the internet and often off on 25 GbE.

L4.prompt_tpl: Transfer {mb} MiB over a link at {bw} MB per second. Give the transfer time in ms, then give it again assuming {ratio} to 1 compression with a decompressor running at 150 MB per second. Answer with the raw transfer time in milliseconds.
L4.answer: raw $= mb \times 1.048576 / bw \times 1000$ ms; compressed $= $ raw$/ratio + mb \times 1.048576/150 \times 1000$ ms. mb=1,bw=125,ratio=3: 8.39 raw vs 2.80+6.99 = 9.79 compressed, so compression loses. mb=10,bw=10,ratio=3: 1048.6 raw vs 349.5+69.9 = 419.4, compression wins. mb=100,bw=1250,ratio=5: 83.9 raw vs 16.8+699.1 = 715.9, compression loses badly.
L4.explanation: The decompression term is proportional to the uncompressed size and does not shrink with the ratio, so it dominates on fast links. This is the arithmetic behind 'compress over the WAN, do not compress over NVLink'.

L4.prompt_tpl: Derive the link bandwidth at which compressing at ratio {ratio} to 1 stops helping, given a decompressor at {dec} MB per second.
L4.answer: Break even when $S/B = S/(rB) + S/D$, so $1/B (1 - 1/r) = 1/D$ and $B = D(1 - 1/r)$. ratio=3,dec=150: 100 MB/s. ratio=5,dec=150: 120 MB/s. ratio=2,dec=800: 400 MB/s.
L4.explanation: Size cancels entirely, so the threshold is a property of the codec and the link, not of the payload. A faster decompressor such as LZ4 at several hundred MB/s pushes the threshold up, which is why LZ4 is the default for internal traffic and gzip is not.

sections.note: the arithmetic behind every capacity argument

L0.body:
L = lambda * W

  L       mean number of items in the system (in flight)
  lambda  mean arrival rate (and, in steady state, departure rate)
  W       mean time an item spends in the system

  35000 rps * 0.040 s  = 1400 requests in flight
  12000 rps * 0.250 s  = 3000 in flight
   8000 rps * 0.025 s  =  200 in flight  -> 200 threads if thread-per-request

No distributional assumptions. Any arrival process, any service order.
L0.cloze: Little's Law is $L = \lambda W$: items in the system equal {{c1::arrival rate}} times {{c2::time in system}}. It assumes {{c3::nothing}} about the arrival or service distribution, only {{c4::steady state}}.

concepts.L1: In any stable system, the mean number of items inside equals the mean arrival rate times the mean time each item spends inside. Written $L = \lambda W$, proved by Little in 1961, and true regardless of arrival or service distribution.
concepts.L2: Its power is that it converts between quantities you can measure and quantities you cannot. You rarely measure concurrency directly, but you always have request rate and latency, and their product is concurrency: connection pool size, thread count, and in-flight memory all fall out of it.
concepts.L3: The law needs only that the system is stable, meaning nothing accumulates without bound, which makes it unusually robust: no exponential assumption, no FIFO assumption, no independence assumption. A service at 8000 requests per second with 25 ms mean latency has 200 requests in flight, so a thread-per-request server needs at least 200 threads and a connection pool below 200 is the bottleneck rather than the database. It also runs in reverse, and that is where it bites: if latency degrades from 25 ms to 250 ms while arrivals hold, in-flight count goes from 200 to 2000, buffer memory grows tenfold, and a fixed thread pool starts rejecting.

L4.prompt_tpl: A service handles {q} requests per second with mean latency {ms} ms. Give the mean number of in-flight requests, and the minimum thread count for a thread-per-request server. Answer with the mean number of in-flight requests.
L4.answer: $L = \lambda W$ with $W$ in seconds. q=8000,ms=25: 200. q=35000,ms=40: 1400. q=500,ms=2000: 1000. Threads must be at least $L$, and in practice above it to absorb variance.
L4.explanation: The third case is the instructive one: only 500 requests per second, but two-second latency means a thousand concurrent requests. Slow endpoints consume concurrency out of all proportion to their traffic share.

L4.prompt_tpl: Arrival rate is fixed at {q} per second. Latency degrades from {a} ms to {b} ms. Derive the change in in-flight requests and explain the memory consequence if each in-flight request holds {kb} KiB of buffers. Answer with the in-flight requests after the degradation.
L4.answer: $L$ scales linearly with $W$. q=8000, 25 to 250 ms: 200 to 2000 in flight, so at 64 KiB each, 12.8 MiB to 128 MiB. q=2000, 50 to 800 ms: 100 to 1600, at 256 KiB each, 25 MiB to 400 MiB. The multiplier on memory equals the multiplier on latency.
L4.explanation: This is the mechanism behind the classic cascade: a dependency slows down, in-flight count rises proportionally, buffer memory rises with it, the process hits its heap limit and dies, and the traffic it was serving moves to its peers.

concepts.t: Utilisation and the M/M/1 response curve

L0.body:
Single server, Poisson arrivals, exponential service, service time S:

  rho = lambda / mu           utilisation, must be < 1
  R   = S / (1 - rho)         mean response time
  Wq  = S * rho / (1 - rho)   mean time queued
  L   = rho / (1 - rho)       mean number in system

With S = 10 ms:
  rho 0.50   R =  20 ms   ( 2.0x S)   L = 1.0
  rho 0.70   R =  33 ms   ( 3.3x S)   L = 2.3
  rho 0.80   R =  50 ms   ( 5.0x S)   L = 4.0
  rho 0.90   R = 100 ms   (10.0x S)   L = 9.0
  rho 0.95   R = 200 ms   (20.0x S)   L = 19.0
  rho 0.99   R = 1000 ms  ( 100x S)   L = 99.0
L0.cloze: For M/M/1, response time is $S/(1-\rho)$ and queue length is $\rho/(1-\rho)$. At $\rho = 0.9$ response time is {{c1::10}} times service time; at $\rho = 0.99$ it is {{c2::100}} times. The curve is a {{c3::hyperbola}}, not a line.

concepts.L1: For a single-server queue with Poisson arrivals and exponential service, mean response time is service time divided by one minus utilisation. The relationship is hyperbolic: response time goes to infinity as utilisation approaches one.
concepts.L2: Utilisation is therefore not a performance metric, it is a distance-to-cliff metric. Going from 50 to 60 percent utilisation costs 25 percent more latency; going from 90 to 95 percent doubles it. The same 10-point step has wildly different consequences depending on where you are.
concepts.L3: Derive it from Little's Law. In M/M/1 the mean number in system is $L = \rho/(1-\rho)$, and Little's Law gives $R = L/\lambda$. With $\lambda = \rho\mu$ and $S = 1/\mu$, this is $S/(1-\rho)$, and the whole behaviour sits in that factor. Two consequences. A capacity plan expressed as a utilisation target is implicitly a latency plan, and 70 versus 90 percent is a 3x difference on identical hardware. And efficiency work gets amplified: halving $S$ at $\rho = 0.9$ takes $\rho$ to 0.45 and response time from 10S to 0.91S, a 22x gain from a 2x speedup. That amplification runs backwards as traffic grows, which is why such gains quietly evaporate.

L4.prompt_tpl: An M/M/1 server has mean service time {s} ms and utilisation {rho}. Give mean response time, mean queueing time, and mean number in system. Answer with the mean response time in milliseconds.
L4.explanation: At high utilisation almost all of the response time is queueing rather than service: at 0.95 utilisation 95 percent of the wait is queue. Optimising the service path is nearly useless in that regime; reducing load or adding servers is the only lever.

L4.prompt_tpl: An efficiency project halves service time from {s} ms to {s2} ms while arrival rate stays fixed at a level that produced utilisation {rho}. Derive the new utilisation and the ratio of old to new mean response time. Answer with the ratio of old to new mean response time.
L4.explanation: A 2x speedup buys 11x latency at 0.9 utilisation and only 3x at 0.5. The benefit of efficiency work is largest exactly where the system is most stressed, and it is destroyed by any traffic growth that restores the old utilisation.

concepts.t: The 80 percent rule, and why headroom is not waste

L0.body:
Marginal cost of one more point of utilisation, M/M/1, R = S/(1-rho):

  rho 0.50 -> 0.51   R  2.000S ->  2.041S    +2.0 percent
  rho 0.80 -> 0.81   R  5.000S ->  5.263S    +5.3 percent
  rho 0.90 -> 0.91   R 10.000S -> 11.111S   +11.1 percent
  rho 0.95 -> 0.96   R 20.000S -> 25.000S   +25.0 percent

Failure headroom, N machines at utilisation rho, one machine lost:
  new rho = rho * N / (N - 1)
  N = 10, rho = 0.80  ->  0.889   survivable
  N = 10, rho = 0.95  ->  1.056   overloaded, cascade
  N =  4, rho = 0.80  ->  1.067   overloaded
L0.cloze: Losing one of $N$ machines raises utilisation to $\rho N/(N-1)$. At $N = 10$ and $\rho = 0.95$ that is {{c1::1.056}}, which is above {{c2::1}} and therefore a {{c3::cascading failure}}, not a slowdown.

concepts.L1: Running above roughly 80 percent utilisation is a design error in most serving systems, for two independent reasons: the response-time derivative is already steep there, and there is no longer enough spare capacity to absorb the loss of a machine.
concepts.L2: The failure-headroom constraint usually binds before the latency one, and it depends on fleet size. Ten machines at 80 percent survive one loss at 89 percent; four machines at 80 percent do not survive it at all, because the survivors are asked for 107 percent of their capacity.
concepts.L3: Two independent arguments both land near 80 percent. The latency one is the derivative of $S/(1-\rho)$, namely $S/(1-\rho)^{2}$: at $\rho = 0.5$ one more point costs 2 percent more latency, at 0.8 it costs 5.3 percent, at 0.95 it costs 25 percent. The availability one is arithmetic on failure: with $N$ machines at $\rho$, losing one leaves $\rho N/(N-1)$, which must stay below 1, so $\rho < (N-1)/N$. For $N = 10$ the ceiling is 0.9, for $N = 4$ it is 0.75. Small fleets need far more headroom per machine, and surviving one zone of three drops the ceiling to two thirds.

L4.prompt_tpl: A fleet of {N} machines runs at utilisation {rho}. Compute the utilisation of the survivors after losing one machine, and after losing one of {az} availability zones. Answer with the survivors' utilisation after losing one machine.
L4.answer: one machine: $\rho N/(N-1)$; one AZ of $z$: $\rho z/(z-1)$. N=10,rho=0.8: 0.889 survivable; AZ of 3: 1.200 overloaded. N=4,rho=0.8: 1.067 overloaded. N=100,rho=0.95: 0.960 survivable; AZ of 3: 1.425 overloaded.
L4.explanation: Zone loss is the constraint that actually binds. Surviving one of three zones caps steady-state utilisation at two thirds regardless of fleet size, which is why well-run multi-AZ services look badly underutilised on a dashboard.

L4.prompt_tpl: Derive the maximum steady-state utilisation for a fleet that must survive {k} simultaneous machine losses out of {N}, and evaluate it.
L4.explanation: This is the ceiling for the queue merely staying stable, with response time going to infinity at exactly that point. A workable target is comfortably below it, which is how 80 percent becomes the folk number for a ten-machine fleet tolerating one loss.

prereqs: Utilisation and the M/M/1 response curve

concepts.t: M/M/c and why one big pool wins

L0.body:
c servers sharing one queue. Erlang C gives P(wait):

  a = lambda / mu          offered load in erlangs
  rho = a / c              per-server utilisation
  C(c, a) = P(an arrival must wait)
  Wq / S  = C(c, a) / (c * (1 - rho))

Same 80 percent per-server utilisation, different pool sizes:
  c =  1   P(wait) 0.800   Wq = 4.000 S   R = 5.000 S
  c =  4   P(wait) 0.596   Wq = 0.746 S   R = 1.746 S
  c = 16   P(wait) 0.305   Wq = 0.095 S   R = 1.095 S
  c = 64   P(wait) 0.056   Wq = 0.004 S   R = 1.004 S

Identical utilisation. Response time falls from 5S to 1.004S.
L0.cloze: In M/M/c at fixed per-server utilisation, growing $c$ sharply reduces queueing: at $\rho = 0.8$, response time is {{c1::5}} times service time at $c=1$ and about {{c2::1.004}} times at $c=64$. The mechanism is {{c3::statistical multiplexing}} of bursts.

concepts.L1: With $c$ servers drawing from one shared queue, queueing delay at a fixed per-server utilisation falls sharply as $c$ grows. Erlang C gives the probability an arrival must wait, and it collapses towards zero for large pools.
concepts.L2: This means utilisation is not comparable across systems of different sizes. A 64-server pool at 80 percent has better latency than a 4-server pool at 60 percent, so a utilisation target copied from one service to another of a different size is meaningless.
concepts.L3: A burst arriving at a pool of one has nowhere to go, while the same burst at a pool of 64 is absorbed by whichever servers happen to be idle, and the probability that all 64 are simultaneously busy is far smaller than the probability that one is. Erlang C makes this precise: at $\rho = 0.8$ the wait probability is 0.800 at $c = 1$, 0.305 at $c = 16$ and 0.056 at $c = 64$, and queueing time is that probability over $c(1-\rho)$, so both factors improve together. Two consequences: per-tenant slices sacrifice this multiplexing and must be justified by isolation rather than efficiency, and any balancer that pins a client to one backend rebuilds a pool of one.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compare a single shared pool of {c} servers at utilisation {rho} against {c} independent single-server queues at the same utilisation. Give response time in units of service time for each and the ratio. Answer with the independent single-server response time in units of service time.
L4.answer: Shared uses Erlang C: c=4,rho=0.8 gives R=1.746S; c=16,rho=0.8 gives 1.095S; c=64,rho=0.8 gives 1.004S; c=4,rho=0.9 gives 2.969S; c=16,rho=0.9 gives 1.370S; c=64,rho=0.9 gives 1.049S. Independent M/M/1 at rho=0.8 is 5.000S and at rho=0.9 is 10.000S. Ratios at rho=0.8: 2.9x, 4.6x, 5.0x.
L4.explanation: Splitting a shared queue into per-server queues costs up to a 5x latency penalty at 80 percent utilisation and 10x at 90 percent, for free, purely from losing multiplexing. This is the strongest argument against sticky routing without a caching reason.

L4.prompt_tpl: A platform team proposes giving each of {t} tenants a dedicated pool of {c} servers instead of one shared pool of the same total size, at the same aggregate utilisation. State what is gained and what is lost, in queueing terms.
L4.answer: Gained: blast-radius isolation, since one tenant's overload is confined to its own pool, plus predictable per-tenant capacity and simpler chargeback. Lost: the multiplexing benefit. Small pools have a much higher wait probability at the same utilisation, so either latency degrades or every pool must be over-provisioned, raising total cost. Shuffle sharding is the middle position: overlapping subsets keep some multiplexing while bounding blast radius.
L4.explanation: Isolation and efficiency are directly opposed here and Erlang C quantifies the exchange rate. Naming shuffle sharding as the compromise is the detail that distinguishes someone who has run a multi-tenant platform.

prereqs: Utilisation and the M/M/1 response curve

concepts.t: Percentiles, and what p99 is not

L0.body:
p99 = the value below which 99 percent of observations fall

It is NOT:
  the latency of 99 percent of users        (one user makes many requests)
  averageable across servers                (mean of p99s is not the p99)
  averageable across time buckets           (same reason)
  meaningful with 50 samples                (p99 of 50 samples is the max)

Correct aggregation: merge histograms, then read the quantile.
Wrong: avg(p99_server_a, p99_server_b).

Sample-count floor: to estimate p99 you need on the order of 1000
samples per window for a stable answer, and 10000 for p99.9.
L0.cloze: The mean of per-server p99s is {{c1::not}} the fleet p99; you must merge {{c2::histograms}} first. Estimating p99 needs on the order of {{c3::1000}} samples in the window.

concepts.L1: A percentile is a quantile of a distribution of individual observations. It does not decompose linearly, so it cannot be averaged across servers, across time windows, or across shards without merging the underlying distributions first.
concepts.L2: Almost every dashboard that shows a fleet-wide p99 computes it wrongly, by averaging per-instance percentiles. The result is systematically optimistic, because averaging pulls the fleet value towards the median of the per-server tails rather than the tail of the merged distribution.
concepts.L3: Consider two servers over one minute. Server A serves 10000 requests with p99 of 20 ms. Server B serves 100 requests, all slow, with p99 of 900 ms. The average of the percentiles is 460 ms, which describes nothing. The merged p99 is dominated by A's volume: of 10100 requests the slowest 101 form the boundary, and B contributes at most 100 of them, so the real value lands near 900 ms here and near 20 ms if B had served only 10 requests. Only the merged distribution answers it, which is why instrumentation should emit histograms with fixed buckets rather than pre-computed percentiles: histograms merge, percentiles do not.

L4.prompt_tpl: A dashboard computes fleet p99 as the mean of {n} per-instance p99 values. Explain the bug, construct a case where the reported value is wrong by more than {f}x, and give the fix.
L4.answer: Percentiles are not linear functionals, so the mean of quantiles is not the quantile of the mixture. Construct: one instance takes almost all traffic and is fast at p99 of 20 ms, while the rest are nearly idle and slow at p99 of 2000 ms. The mean of the p99s approaches 2000 ms while the true merged p99 is near 20 ms, a 100x error. The fix is to export mergeable histograms and compute the quantile after summing bucket counts.
L4.explanation: The error goes in both directions depending on how traffic is distributed across instances, which is worse than a consistent bias because it changes sign as load shifts.

L4.prompt_tpl: A service receives {q} requests per second and you aggregate over a {w} second window. How many samples per window, and which of p50, p99, p99.9 and p99.99 can be estimated from it? Answer with the number of samples per window.
L4.answer: samples $= q \times w$. q=50,w=10: 500 samples, so p50 and p99 are usable and p99.9 rests on fewer than one expected observation. q=5000,w=60: 300000, all four are fine. q=3,w=60: 180 samples, only p50 is meaningful and p99 is effectively the second-largest value.
L4.explanation: A percentile needs roughly 10 expected observations beyond it to be stable, so p99 needs about 1000 samples and p99.9 about 10000. Low-traffic services genuinely cannot have a p99.9 SLO on a short window, which is a real constraint on SLO design.

L0.body:
One request fans out to n backends and waits for all of them.
If each backend independently exceeds T with probability p:

  P(request exceeds T) = 1 - (1 - p)^n

  p = 0.01 (per-backend p99):
    n =   1    1.0 percent
    n =  10    9.6 percent
    n = 100   63.4 percent      <- your p99 is now the median
    n = 200   86.6 percent

Inverted: to hold a 1 percent overall miss rate at n backends,
each backend needs per-request tail q where q^n = 0.99:
    n =  10 -> p99.8995 per backend
    n = 100 -> p99.99   per backend
L0.cloze: Fanning out to $n$ backends and waiting for all gives $P = 1 - (1-p)^{n}$. At $p = 0.01$ and $n = 100$ that is {{c1::63.4}} percent, so to keep an overall 1 percent tail at $n = 100$ each backend must hold {{c2::p99.99}}.

concepts.L1: When a request must wait for $n$ independent backends, the probability it is slow is $1 - (1-p)^{n}$, where $p$ is each backend's probability of being slow. Modest per-backend tails become the common case at scale.
concepts.L2: The consequence is that per-service SLOs do not compose. A backend meeting a 99th-percentile target is contributing a 63 percent slow rate to a request that touches 100 such backends, so scatter-gather systems must set backend targets from the fan-out, not from what feels reasonable in isolation.
concepts.L3: This is the core arithmetic of Dean and Barroso's The Tail at Scale. Independence is the key assumption and it is optimistic: correlated slowness from a shared network, a power event, or synchronised garbage collection makes the real number worse, because events cluster rather than cancelling. The design responses fall into three families. Reduce $n$ by partitioning coarsely or caching so fewer shards are touched. Reduce $p$ per backend, which is expensive because the required percentile grows towards $0.99^{1/n}$. Or break the all-of-$n$ dependency: return partial results when a shard is late, or hedge so a slow replica is raced rather than waited on.

L4.prompt_tpl: A query scatters to {n} shards and waits for all. Each shard independently exceeds the deadline with probability {p}. Give the probability the query misses its deadline.
L4.explanation: Note that n=10 at p=0.01 and n=100 at p=0.001 give the same 9.5 percent: the product $np$ governs the small-probability regime. That approximation breaks once $np$ approaches 1.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need overall deadline misses at or below {target} percent for a query fanning out to {n} shards. Derive the per-shard tail probability required and express it as a percentile. Answer with the required per-shard tail probability.
L4.explanation: The required per-shard percentile gains roughly one nine per factor of ten in fan-out. Beyond about a thousand shards this is unachievable, which is why large scatter-gather systems return partial results rather than chasing more nines.

prereqs: Percentiles, and what p99 is not

L0.body:
HEDGED: send to replica 2 if replica 1 has not answered by the p95 deadline.
  extra load = fraction of requests that hedge = 0.05
  tail seen  = P(both slow) instead of P(one slow)
  p = 0.05 independent -> 0.0025, roughly p99.75 from a p95 backend

TIED: send to both immediately, each carrying the other's identity.
  whichever dequeues first cancels its twin
  extra load approaches 2x in queue-entry cost, near 0 in work done

Budget rule: cap hedging at a small percentage of total requests, else
the hedge traffic is itself the overload that caused the tail.
L0.cloze: A hedged request is issued only after the first attempt passes the {{c1::p95}} deadline, so it costs about {{c2::5}} percent extra load and squares the slow probability. A {{c3::tied}} request is sent to both replicas at once with mutual cancellation.

concepts.L1: Two techniques from The Tail at Scale for cutting tail latency without making any backend faster: send a second copy of a request after a short delay (hedging), or send both immediately with cross-cancellation (tying).
concepts.L2: Hedging works because the slow events are largely independent and transient, so a second attempt usually lands on a healthy path. It fails exactly when they are correlated, and in that case the extra load makes the overload worse, so hedging must be strictly budgeted.
concepts.L3: Set the hedge deadline at the backend's p95 and only 5 percent of requests produce a second call, so the cost is 5 percent extra load. The benefit is that a request is slow only if both attempts are slow: at independence $0.05^{2} = 0.0025$, turning a p95 backend into an effective p99.75. Tied requests remove the delay entirely: both copies enter queues at once and the first to reach a head cancels the other, so the client pays the shorter queue. The property that matters is the budget. Unbudgeted hedging under real overload doubles offered load exactly when the system cannot take it, which is the retry-storm failure shape again.

L4.prompt_tpl: A backend is hedged at its p{pct} deadline against {r} replicas, with independent slowness. Give the extra load fraction and the resulting probability that a request is slow. Answer with the probability that a request is slow.
L4.answer: extra load $= p = 1 - pct/100$; slow probability $= p^{r}$. pct=95,r=2: 5 percent extra, 0.0025 slow, effectively p99.75. pct=99,r=2: 1 percent extra, 0.0001, p99.99. pct=90,r=3: 10 percent extra, 0.001, p99.9.
L4.explanation: Hedging late is cheap and helps less; hedging early is expensive and helps more. Note the independence assumption is doing all the work, and correlated slowness collapses the benefit while keeping the cost.

L4.prompt_tpl: During an incident, backend p99 rises from {a} ms to {b} ms across the whole fleet because of a shared dependency. Predict what an unbudgeted hedging policy set at the old p95 does, and state the correct behaviour.
L4.answer: Nearly every request now exceeds the old p95 deadline, so nearly every request hedges and offered load roughly doubles against a fleet already failing. Hedging converts a latency incident into a capacity incident. Correct behaviour: hedge only while the hedge rate stays under a fixed budget, typically a few percent, disable hedging entirely above it, and derive the deadline from a rolling percentile so it moves with conditions rather than being pinned to a stale value.
L4.explanation: Every duplicate-work tail mitigation is safe under independent failure and dangerous under correlated failure, so all of them need a budget and a kill switch. This is the same structural lesson as retry budgets.

sections.note: how load is placed, limited, and shed

L0.body:
round robin           next in order; ignores load entirely
  weighted round robin  same, with static per-backend weights
  least connections     fewest in-flight; a decent load proxy
  least request / EWMA  fewest outstanding, smoothed over time
  power of two choices  sample 2 at random, take the less loaded
  consistent hashing    key -> ring position; stable under churn
  maglev hashing        consistent, but near-perfectly even

Maximum load above the mean, N backends:
  random single choice  O(log N / log log N)
  two random choices    O(log log N), for one extra sample
L0.cloze: Sampling {{c1::two}} backends at random and taking the less loaded reduces maximum load above the mean from order $\log N / \log\log N$ to order {{c2::$\log\log N$}}, which is why it beats round robin almost everywhere at near-zero cost.

concepts.L1: The choice of which backend receives a request. Options range from stateless round robin through load-aware policies such as least-request and power-of-two-choices, to hash-based policies that deliberately pin keys to backends.
concepts.L2: Round robin is load-blind, so it is optimal only when every request costs the same, which is almost never true. One slow backend under round robin receives exactly as much work as a healthy one and becomes the tail for the whole service.
concepts.L3: Power of two choices is the best default because of a sharp result: with $N$ backends and random single assignment, the most loaded carries $O(\log N / \log\log N)$ more than the mean, whereas sampling two and taking the lesser reduces that to $O(\log\log N)$, an exponential improvement for one extra sample. Least-request approximates the same effect with local state, and an exponentially weighted moving average of latency lets it distinguish a backend that is slow from one that is merely busy. Hash-based policies are a different category: chosen for locality, they explicitly trade even load for stable placement, so they inherit the hot-key problem and need bounded-load variants.

L4.prompt_tpl: One backend out of {N} has degraded to {x}x normal service time but is still accepting connections. Predict what round robin, least-request, and power-of-two-choices each do, and give the resulting share of requests hitting the sick backend.
L4.answer: Round robin sends it exactly 1/N of traffic regardless, so 5 percent at N=20, and every one of those requests is x times slower, which lands squarely in the tail. Least-request sends it far less: outstanding requests pile up on it, so new requests go elsewhere, and its share falls to roughly 1/(N-1+x) of traffic. Power of two choices behaves similarly since it will almost always reject it when sampled against a healthy peer. Only the load-blind policy is fooled.
L4.explanation: Load-aware balancing is a partial substitute for health checking, and it reacts in milliseconds where health checks react in seconds. This is why least-request is the modern default in service meshes.

L4.prompt_tpl: A hash-based balancer maps keys to {N} backends. One key accounts for {pct} percent of all traffic. Give the load on the backend holding it relative to the mean, and name the mitigation. Answer with the relative load on the backend holding the hot key.
L4.answer: relative load $= pct/100 + (1 - pct/100)/N$, divided by the mean of $1/N$, giving $N \cdot pct/100 + 1 - pct/100$. N=64,pct=5: 4.15x mean. N=16,pct=20: 3.99x. N=256,pct=1: 3.55x. Mitigation: bounded-load consistent hashing, key splitting with a random suffix, or a local cache for the hot key.
L4.explanation: Hash balancing gives no protection against key skew, and the relative overload grows linearly with the number of backends because the mean shrinks while the hot key does not. Bounded-load consistent hashing caps each node at a multiple of the mean and spills the remainder.

prereqs: M/M/c and why one big pool wins

L0.body:
HEALTH-CHECK FLAP   the check passes while real traffic fails
  HERD ON RECOVERY    a returning backend is sent all the traffic
  SUCCESSFUL FAILURE  a backend failing fast looks least-loaded, so
                      it wins every routing decision and blackholes
  CASCADING DRAIN     checks fail under load -> removed -> survivors
                      overload -> their checks fail -> fleet empties
  SINGLE-LB SPOF      the LB caps availability of all behind it

Guards: outlier detection on real results, a panic threshold, slow
start on re-entry, connection draining on exit.
L0.cloze: A backend that {{c1::fails fast}} looks least-loaded and attracts all traffic — the successful-failure or black-hole mode. The standard guard is a {{c2::panic threshold}}: past some fraction unhealthy, ignore health checks and load-balance across everything.

concepts.L1: Load balancers introduce their own failure modes, most of which come from acting on stale or misleading health information: black-holing to fast-failing backends, herding on recovery, and cascading drain under load.
concepts.L2: The counterintuitive one is that failing fast makes a backend more attractive to a least-request balancer, because failure lowers its outstanding-request count. Without success-rate-aware outlier detection the sickest node reliably wins every routing decision.
concepts.L3: Cascading drain is the mode that takes whole services down, and its mechanism is a feedback loop. Health checks usually have a latency component, so under load a healthy-but-busy backend starts failing checks; the balancer removes it; the same load falls on fewer backends; by the M/M/1 curve their latency multiplies; their checks fail too. The fleet empties in seconds while every process is alive. Two guards break the loop. A panic threshold says that once more than about half the hosts look unhealthy the signal is probably wrong, so route to everything. And health checks should test liveness cheaply, leaving load-based removal to ejection-limited outlier detection.

L4.prompt_tpl: A fleet of {N} backends runs at {rho} utilisation. The health check has a {ms} ms timeout and shares the request path. Traffic rises 20 percent. Trace what happens and name the two mitigations.
L4.answer: Utilisation goes to 0.96 at rho=0.8, so by $S/(1-\rho)$ response time roughly quintuples and health checks start exceeding the timeout. Hosts are ejected; the remaining hosts absorb their load and pass utilisation 1.0, so their checks fail too; the fleet drains completely while every process is healthy. Mitigations: a panic threshold that ignores health once a large fraction appear unhealthy, and health checks that do not traverse the loaded request path or that have no latency component.
L4.explanation: The bug is a positive feedback loop between load and health, and it is why health checking must be decoupled from the resource under contention. Load shedding is the correct response to overload; ejection is not.

L4.prompt_tpl: A backend returns HTTP 503 in {ms} ms for every request while healthy peers take {p} ms. Explain what a least-request balancer does and give the correct policy.
L4.answer: The failing backend has near-zero outstanding requests because it drains its queue instantly, so least-request considers it the least loaded and routes essentially all traffic to it, black-holing the service. Correct policy: outlier detection on success rate, not just on latency or connection count, with ejection based on consecutive errors or a success-rate deviation from the fleet, plus a cap on the fraction of hosts that may be ejected at once.
L4.explanation: Any load metric that treats fast failure as low load is exploitable by the failure itself. Success rate must be part of the routing signal, which is exactly why service meshes ship outlier detection separately from load balancing.

L0.body:
state: tokens (float), last_refill (timestamp)
  params: B = burst capacity, r = refill rate per second

  on request of cost k:
     now = clock()
     tokens = min(B, tokens + (now - last_refill) * r)
     last_refill = now
     if tokens >= k: tokens -= k; ALLOW
     else:           DENY, retry after (k - tokens)/r seconds

  B = 100, r = 10/s:
     max requests in any window of T seconds = B + r*T
     T = 30 -> 100 + 300 = 400   (average 13.3/s over the window)
     sustained rate = 10/s;  full-bucket recovery = B/r = 10 s
L0.cloze: Token bucket allows at most {{c1::B + rT}} requests in any window of length $T$: the {{c2::burst}} capacity plus the refill over the window. Sustained rate is {{c3::r}} and the bucket refills fully in {{c4::B/r}} seconds.

concepts.L1: A rate limiter holding up to $B$ tokens that refill at $r$ per second. A request consumes tokens if available and is denied otherwise, so the limiter permits bursts up to $B$ while enforcing a long-run rate of $r$.
concepts.L2: The advertised limit is the sustained rate $r$, but the actual worst case a downstream service must absorb is $B + rT$ over any window $T$. Sizing capacity from the advertised rate and ignoring the burst term is how limiters that are correctly configured still cause overload.
concepts.L3: Two parameters, two independent properties, usually confused. $r$ sets fairness over long horizons and $B$ sets tolerance for legitimate bursts, such as a client batching a page load into twenty parallel calls. The maximum admitted in any window of length $T$ is $B + rT$, so with $B = 100$ and $r = 10$ per second a 30-second window admits 400 requests, 33 percent above the advertised limit. The burst term amortises away over longer windows, and short-window behaviour is what decides whether a backend survives. The distributed implementation is where correctness is lost: the read-modify-write must be atomic, so a Redis Lua script, not GET then SET.

L4.prompt_tpl: A token bucket has burst capacity {B} and refill rate {r} per second, starting full. Give the maximum number of requests admitted over {T} seconds, the effective average rate over that window, and the percentage above the advertised limit. Answer with the maximum number of requests admitted.
L4.answer: max $= B + rT$; average $= (B + rT)/T$; excess $= B/(rT)$. B=100,r=10,T=30: 400, 13.33/s, 33.3 percent above. B=1000,r=200,T=10: 3000, 300/s, 50 percent above. B=20,r=5,T=1: 25, 25/s, 400 percent above.
L4.explanation: The excess is $B/(rT)$, so the burst matters enormously on short windows and vanishes on long ones. Size the downstream for the shortest window that can hurt it, which is usually about one service time.

L4.prompt_tpl: A distributed limiter implements token bucket as Redis GET, compute, SET, with {n} application instances. Describe the failure and give the fix and its cost.
L4.answer: GET and SET are not atomic together, so concurrent instances read the same token count and each independently decides to allow, then overwrite each other's decrement. Under contention the effective limit approaches $n$ times the configured limit. Fix: a Lua script executing the read, refill, compare and decrement atomically on the Redis server, or an atomic DECR against a pre-refilled counter. Cost: one network round trip per request on the hot path, plus Redis becoming a hard dependency of every request.
L4.explanation: Lost-update on a shared counter is the classic distributed rate-limiter bug and it scales with instance count, so it is invisible in a two-instance test environment and severe in production.

concepts.t: Leaky bucket and the sliding window counter

L0.body:
LEAKY BUCKET (a queue): requests enter a fixed-size FIFO, drain at r/s.
  admits at a constant rate; no burst passes through
  overflow -> drop. Adds latency up to queue_size / r seconds

FIXED WINDOW: count per wall-clock window, limit L.
  L requests at 0:59 plus L at 1:00 = 2L in one second

SLIDING WINDOW LOG: a timestamp per request; exact, O(L) per key.
  1M keys at limit 1000, 8 B per timestamp = 8 GB.

SLIDING WINDOW COUNTER: two counters plus interpolation.
  est = prev * (1 - elapsed_fraction) + cur
  prev=100, cur=60, elapsed=25 percent -> 135. Two integers per key.
L0.cloze: Fixed windows allow {{c1::2L}} across a boundary. The sliding window counter estimates $prev \times (1 - f) + cur$ where $f$ is the {{c2::elapsed fraction}} of the current window, using {{c3::two}} integers per key instead of a full log.

concepts.L1: Three alternatives to token bucket. Leaky bucket smooths output to a constant rate by queueing; fixed windows are cheap and wrong at boundaries; the sliding window counter interpolates between two windows for near-exact accuracy at constant memory.
concepts.L2: Leaky bucket and token bucket are often described as equivalent and are not: token bucket lets a burst through immediately, leaky bucket never does, and leaky bucket adds queueing delay that token bucket does not. Choosing between them is choosing whether bursts are absorbed or paced.
concepts.L3: The sliding window counter is the design worth being able to derive. A fixed window of limit $L$ admits up to $2L$ in a single second when a client places $L$ requests just before a boundary and $L$ just after. A sliding log fixes it exactly by storing every timestamp, at $O(L)$ memory per key: one million keys at a limit of 1000 with 8-byte timestamps is 8 GB, which is why nobody deploys it at scale. The counter keeps only the previous and current window totals and weights the previous by the fraction still inside the trailing window, giving $prev(1-f) + cur$. Its error comes from assuming uniformity within the previous window, so it overcounts an early burst and undercounts a late one.

L4.prompt_tpl: Sliding window counter with limit {L} per minute. The previous minute recorded {prev} requests, the current minute has recorded {cur}, and {f} percent of the current minute has elapsed. Give the estimate and the decision. Answer with the estimate.
L4.answer: est $= prev(1-f/100) + cur$. prev=100,cur=60,f=25: 135, so denied at L=100 and allowed at L=500. prev=80,cur=50,f=70: 74, allowed at L=100. prev=20,cur=400,f=99: 400.2, denied at L=100 and denied at L=500 only if the limit is 400 or lower; at L=500 it is allowed.
L4.explanation: As $f$ approaches 100 percent the previous window's contribution decays to nothing, so the estimate converges to a pure fixed-window count at the moment of the boundary. That residual is the source of the remaining approximation error.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compare memory for a sliding window log versus a sliding window counter for {k} million keys at a limit of {L} per window, with 8 bytes per timestamp and 4 bytes per counter. Answer with the sliding window log memory in bytes.
L4.answer: log $= k \times 10^{6} \times L \times 8$ bytes; counter $= k \times 10^{6} \times 2 \times 4$ bytes. k=1,L=1000: 8 GB versus 8 MB, a 1000x saving. k=10,L=100: 8 GB versus 80 MB, 100x. k=0.1,L=1000: 0.8 GB versus 0.8 MB, 1000x.
L4.explanation: The ratio is exactly $L$ times the ratio of element sizes, so the log becomes infeasible precisely for the high-limit keys you most want to track. That memory argument, not accuracy, is why the counter is the production choice.

L0.body:
Three states, with the thresholds that move between them:

  CLOSED     calls pass. Track failures over a rolling window.
             trip when failures/total > threshold AND total >= min_volume
  OPEN       calls fail immediately; no request is sent.
             after open_duration, move to HALF_OPEN
  HALF_OPEN  allow k probes. All succeed -> CLOSED; any fail -> OPEN

  25 of 200 = 0.125 > 0.10 threshold, volume >= 20 -> OPEN
   4 of  50 = 0.080 > 0.05 threshold, volume >= 20 -> OPEN
   2 of   5 = 0.400 but volume 5 < 20 -> stays CLOSED
L0.cloze: A breaker trips only when the failure ratio exceeds the threshold {{c1::and}} the request volume exceeds a minimum, so a small sample cannot trip it. It recovers through a {{c2::half-open}} state that admits a few probe calls.

concepts.L1: A state machine wrapping a remote call. After enough failures within a rolling window it stops issuing calls entirely for a period, then admits a few probes before closing again. Named and popularised by Michael Nygard in Release It.
concepts.L2: Its real purpose is not protecting the caller from errors, it is protecting the callee from load and the caller from holding threads on doomed calls. Yet it does this by converting partial failure into total failure, which is the opposite of what a system designed for graceful degradation wants.
concepts.L3: Marc Brooker's objection is the one worth being able to state. Consider a service sharded so keys A through H live on one shard. That shard is overloaded, so 12 percent of requests fail. A client-side breaker sees 12 percent, exceeds its threshold, and opens, now failing 100 percent including the 88 percent that would have succeeded. The breaker made the outage eight times worse. It only helps when failure is all-or-nothing from the caller's view, true for a dead process and false for a hot shard. Prefer per-shard breakers, keep timeouts and bounded concurrency as the primary protection, and treat the breaker as an optimisation.

L4.prompt_tpl: A breaker has failure threshold {th} and minimum volume {mv}. Given {f} failures in {n} calls, state whether it trips and give the failure ratio. Answer with the failure ratio.
L4.answer: ratio $= f/n$; trips iff ratio > th and $n \geq mv$. f=25,n=200: 0.125, trips at th=0.1 and mv=20 or 100. f=4,n=50: 0.08, trips at th=0.05 with mv=20, not with mv=100. f=2,n=5: 0.40, never trips at mv=20 or 100 despite the high ratio.
L4.explanation: The minimum-volume gate is what stops a low-traffic endpoint from tripping on statistical noise. Without it, a path receiving three requests a minute will open its breaker regularly for no reason.

L4.prompt_tpl: A service is sharded {s} ways and one shard is overloaded, failing all its requests. A client-side breaker has threshold {th}. Predict the effect and give the better design.
L4.answer: Failure rate is $1/s$: 12.5 percent at 8 shards, 1.6 percent at 64. At 8 shards it exceeds both thresholds, so the breaker opens and converts a 12.5 percent failure into a 100 percent failure, an eightfold amplification. At 64 shards it exceeds 0.05 marginally and not 0.1. Better design: shard-aware breakers so only the sick partition is broken, plus timeouts and bounded per-dependency concurrency, which limit thread consumption without discarding healthy traffic.
L4.explanation: Circuit breakers assume the failure signal is representative of the whole callee, which sharding violates by construction. The amplification factor is exactly the number of shards, so breakers get more dangerous as you shard more finely.

L0.body:
BULKHEAD: a separate resource pool per dependency, so one cannot starve
the rest.
  pool A: 20 threads for payments;  pool B: 20 threads for search
  search hangs -> 20 threads blocked, payments unaffected
  without it: all 200 threads block on search; the service is down

SHUFFLE SHARDING: give each tenant a random subset of k nodes from n.
  distinct assignments = C(n, k);  n = 100, k = 2 -> 4950
  P(two tenants fully overlap) = 1 / C(n, k) = 0.0002
  an abusive tenant fully takes out only tenants sharing both nodes
L0.cloze: A bulkhead gives each dependency its own {{c1::resource pool}} so one hang cannot consume all threads. Shuffle sharding assigns each tenant {{c2::k of n}} nodes, giving {{c3::C(n, k)}} distinct assignments and a tiny probability of full overlap.

concepts.L1: Two isolation patterns. Bulkheads partition a caller's resources per dependency so a single hanging dependency cannot consume all threads or connections. Shuffle sharding assigns each tenant a random subset of nodes so blast radius is bounded combinatorially.
concepts.L2: Bulkheads are what actually saves you when a dependency hangs, not circuit breakers, because the damage from a hang is thread exhaustion and it happens before any failure signal exists to trip a breaker. A hung call never returns an error to count.
concepts.L3: The bulkhead argument follows from Little's Law. A service at 500 requests per second calling a dependency that normally takes 20 ms holds $500 \times 0.02 = 10$ threads on that path. If the dependency hangs until a 30-second timeout that becomes 15000 threads demanded, so any shared pool is exhausted in a fraction of a second and every unrelated endpoint stops. Capping the pool at 50 makes the blast radius exactly 50 threads and the excess fails fast on pool acquisition. Shuffle sharding solves the multi-tenant version: with $n = 100$ and $k = 2$ there are $\binom{100}{2} = 4950$ assignments, so an abusive tenant fully overlaps about 1 in 4950 others.

L4.prompt_tpl: A service takes {q} requests per second on a dependency that normally responds in {ms} ms but hangs until a {to} second timeout. Give normal and hung thread demand, and the bulkhead size that caps damage at {cap} percent of a {pool}-thread pool. Answer with the hung thread demand.
L4.answer: normal $= q \times ms/1000$; hung $= q \times to$; bulkhead $= pool \times cap/100$. q=500,ms=20: 10 threads normally; to=30: 15000 demanded. cap=25,pool=200: bulkhead 50. q=2000,ms=5: 10 normally; to=10: 20000 demanded; cap=10,pool=1000: bulkhead 100.
L4.explanation: Note that normal demand is tiny and hung demand is unbounded by anything except the timeout. That ratio, here 1500x, is why an unbounded shared pool always loses and why the bulkhead size can be small without hurting the healthy path.

L4.prompt_tpl: Shuffle sharding assigns each tenant {k} nodes at random from {n}. Give the number of distinct assignments and the probability that a given tenant shares both nodes with a specific abusive tenant. Answer with the number of distinct assignments.
L4.answer: assignments $= \binom{n}{k}$; full-overlap probability $= 1/\binom{n}{k}$. n=100,k=2: 4950 and 0.000202. n=20,k=2: 190 and 0.00526. n=500,k=3: 20708500 and about $4.8 \times 10^{-8}$. n=100,k=3: 161700 and 0.0000062.
L4.explanation: Blast radius shrinks combinatorially in $k$, so moving from two nodes per tenant to three cuts full overlap by a factor of 33 at n=100. The cost is that each tenant's traffic is spread more thinly, which reduces cache locality.

L0.body:
Naive retries multiply through call depth:
  attempts per layer a = 3, depth d = 3  ->  a^d = 27 leaf calls per request
  a = 3, d = 4 -> 81      a = 2, d = 5 -> 32

RETRY BUDGET: cap retries as a fraction of successful requests.
  10 percent of 1000 requests -> at most 100 retries in the window
  above budget: fail immediately

BACKOFF WITH JITTER, base b, attempt i, cap c:
  exponential:  min(c, b * 2^i)              all clients retry together
  full jitter:  uniform(0, min(c, b * 2^i))  spread out
  decorrelated: min(c, uniform(b, prev * 3))
L0.cloze: Retries at every layer of a call stack multiply as {{c1::$a^{d}$}}, so 3 attempts over 3 layers is {{c2::27}} leaf calls. The two guards are a retry {{c3::budget}} expressed as a fraction of successes, and {{c4::jitter}} on the backoff.

concepts.L1: Retries at multiple layers of a call chain compound multiplicatively, turning a single client request into $a^{d}$ leaf calls for $a$ attempts across $d$ layers. Budgets bound the total and jitter decorrelates the timing.
concepts.L2: Exponential backoff alone does not prevent a retry storm, it only delays it, because every client that failed at the same instant computes the same delay and retries at the same instant. Randomness, not the exponential, is what spreads the load.
concepts.L3: The amplification arithmetic is what makes this urgent: three attempts per layer across four layers is 81 leaf calls per user request, so a dependency briefly at 110 percent of capacity sees offered load jump by nearly two orders of magnitude and can never recover on its own. Two fixes are needed together. Retry budgets bound retry traffic as a fraction of successes, typically 10 percent, so retries help a transient blip and cannot sustain an overload. Jitter fixes the timing: Brooker's analysis shows full jitter, drawn uniformly from zero to the current cap, cuts total work by more than half at a hundred contending clients. Finally, retry at one layer only, so the exponent is 1.

L4.prompt_tpl: A call chain is {d} layers deep and each layer retries up to {a} times. Give the worst-case leaf calls per user request, and the offered-load multiplier on the leaf service if every layer is retrying. Answer with the worst-case leaf calls per user request.
L4.answer: leaf calls $= a^{d}$, and the multiplier is the same number. d=3,a=3: 27. d=4,a=3: 81. d=5,a=2: 32. d=3,a=2: 8. d=4,a=2: 16. d=5,a=3: 243.
L4.explanation: The exponent is the number of layers that retry, not the number of layers. Restricting retries to a single layer makes the multiplier $a$ rather than $a^{d}$, which is the cheapest available fix and requires no new machinery.

L4.prompt_tpl: A service handles {q} requests per second and a retry budget allows retries up to {pct} percent of successful requests. Derive the maximum retry rate and the total offered load at the moment the budget saturates. Answer with the total offered load.
L4.answer: max retries $= q \times pct/100$; total offered $= q(1 + pct/100)$. q=10000,pct=10: 1000 retries/s, 11000 total. q=10000,pct=20: 2000, 12000. q=500,pct=5: 25, 525.
L4.explanation: The budget converts an unbounded multiplier into a bounded one: total offered load can never exceed $1 + pct/100$ times the base rate no matter how badly the dependency is failing. That bound is the entire point.

cache-aside read:
     v = cache.get(k)
     if v is None:
         v = db.get(k)                # miss
         cache.set(k, v, ttl=300)
     return v

  origin load = QPS * (1 - hit_ratio)
     200000 rps at 0.95 -> 10000 rps to the database   (20x divider)
     200000 rps at 0.99 ->  2000 rps                   (100x divider)

  invalidation choices, in order of increasing precision and risk:
     TTL only      stale up to ttl, cannot fail
     write-through cache updated in the write path; write fails if cache does
     explicit      delete on write; correct until one delete is lost
L0.cloze: Origin load is QPS times {{c1::(1 - hit ratio)}}, so the useful framing is the divider {{c2::1/(1-h)}}: 95 percent is a {{c3::20}}x reduction and 99 percent is a {{c4::100}}x reduction.

concepts.L1: Cache aside with Redis, read replicas, CDN for static and semi-static content, denormalization, materialized views.
concepts.L2: Cache invalidation strategy is the actual question. TTL-based is simple and stale; write-through is consistent and couples writes to cache availability; explicit invalidation is precise and easy to get wrong. Pick one and say why.
concepts.L3: The hit ratio compresses on the wrong scale. Reading 95 and 99 percent as similar numbers hides that the second sends five times less traffic to the origin, because what matters is the miss ratio and its reciprocal. That is why cache work has a sharply increasing return near the top, and why an origin sized for a 99 percent hit ratio has no margin: a cold cache, a flush, or a deploy that changes a key prefix takes origin load from 2000 to 200000 requests per second instantly. The defence is request coalescing so concurrent misses on one key produce one origin call, staggered TTLs, and serving stale data while a refresh is in flight.

L4.prompt_tpl: A cache fronting the database sees {q} requests per second at a {h} percent hit ratio. Give origin load, the load-reduction divider, and origin load if the cache is emptied. Answer with the origin load in requests per second.
L4.explanation: The last column is the incident. A 1000x divider means the origin is provisioned for a thousandth of peak traffic, so any event that empties the cache is an instant thousandfold overload. Cache warming and coalescing are not optional at that ratio.

L4.prompt_tpl: Choose an invalidation strategy for user permissions data changing about {n} times per day per user, where a stale allow is a security incident.
L4.answer: Not TTL alone: any TTL longer than zero means a revoked permission is honoured for up to that long, which is the security incident by definition. Use explicit invalidation on write plus a short TTL as a backstop for lost invalidations, and make the authorisation check fail closed on cache unavailability. If revocation must be immediate, do not cache the decision at all; cache the inputs and evaluate per request.
L4.explanation: Caching decisions for authorisation is the standard example of where staleness is not a performance trade but a correctness violation. Caching the inputs rather than the verdict keeps most of the benefit without the failure mode.

shard_id = hash(shard_key) % N          -> resharding moves ~all keys
  shard_id = consistent_hash(shard_key)   -> resharding moves ~1/N of keys

  cross-shard query cost:
     single-shard  1 network hop
     scatter-gather over N shards: N hops, and tail = max of N
     at per-shard p99 = 0.01 and N = 64: P(slow) = 1 - 0.99^64 = 0.475

  resharding by doubling: N -> 2N, each old shard splits in two

L0.cloze: Modulo sharding moves nearly {{c1::all}} keys on a resharding; consistent hashing moves about {{c2::1/N}}. Splitting by {{c3::doubling}} keeps the move local to the shard being split.

concepts.L1: Sharding, LSM-backed stores, write batching, async processing via queue, event sourcing.
concepts.L2: The hard part of sharding is not the sharding, it's the cross-shard query and the resharding operation. Address both unprompted.
concepts.L3: The write path is rarely the hard part, because LSM-backed stores turn random writes into sequential ones and one node absorbs tens of thousands per second. The hard parts are queries that do not respect the shard key and the day you need more shards. A scatter-gather across 64 shards inherits the tail arithmetic: at a per-shard p99 of 1 percent, 47.5 percent of such queries are slow. Resharding is worse, being an online migration with a correctness requirement, and the sequence is always the same: add the new topology, dual-write, backfill, verify by comparing reads, cut reads over, stop writing to the old. Say that sequence unprompted.

L4.prompt_tpl: A scatter-gather query touches all {N} shards and waits for all. Each shard's slow probability is {p}. Give the query's slow probability, and the same figure if a secondary index lets the query touch only {k} shards. Answer with the slow probability when all shards are touched.

     read  = 1 range scan of a precomputed list     fast

     write = 1 insert                               fast

concepts.L2: The hybrid is the actual production answer and the celebrity problem is the reason. Twitter's published architecture does exactly this.
concepts.L3: Both pure strategies fail on the same distribution from opposite ends. Follower counts are heavy-tailed, so fan-out on write is cheap for the median author and ruinous for the top 0.001 percent; following counts are also skewed, so fan-out on read is cheap for the median reader and expensive for someone following ten thousand accounts. The hybrid works because the two tails are different populations: capping write fan-out bounds the worst write, and since a typical user follows only a handful of accounts above the threshold, the read-time merge is a few extra range scans. POST /payments
  Idempotency-Key: 6f1b2c...     client-generated, e.g. UUIDv4

  server, in one transaction:
     INSERT INTO idem(key, request_hash, state)
       VALUES (:key, :hash, 'in_progress')
     ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING
     RETURNING key;   -- zero rows means someone else has this key

  we inserted:  do the work; UPDATE idem SET state='done', response=...
  we did not:   SELECT state
                  'done'        -> return the stored response
                  'in_progress' -> 409, tell the client to retry
  a different request_hash for the same key -> 422, not a replay
L0.cloze: The race between two concurrent requests with the same key is resolved by a {{c1::unique constraint}} on the key. The loser returns the stored response if the state is done, and a {{c2::409}} if it is still in progress — never re-executing.

concepts.L1: Client-supplied idempotency key, stored with the result, returned on replay. Essential for payments and anything retried.
concepts.L2: The subtlety is the race: two concurrent requests with the same key. You need a unique constraint or a lock, and returning the in-progress state rather than double-executing.
concepts.L3: The naive implementation checks for the key, sees nothing, and proceeds, which is a check-then-act race that duplicates work whenever two retries arrive inside the execution window. The fix is to make the insert itself the mutual exclusion, so exactly one caller wins the unique constraint and the others learn they lost, atomically. Three details separate a correct implementation. The key record must be written in the same transaction as the effect, or a crash between them re-executes. Storing a hash of the request body lets you reject a client reusing a key with different parameters. And the record needs an expiry that exceeds the client's maximum retry horizon.

L4.prompt_tpl: A payments service checks 'SELECT * FROM idem WHERE key = ?', proceeds if empty, and inserts the key after charging. Two retries arrive {ms} ms apart while the charge takes {dur} ms. Describe what happens and give the fix.
L4.answer: Both requests select an empty result because neither has inserted yet, so both charge. Any gap smaller than the charge duration double-charges, which is every case here. Fix: make the insert first and atomic, using an ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING against a unique constraint, so exactly one caller proceeds and the other reads the stored state. Do the insert and the effect in one transaction, or use an outbox if the effect is external.
L4.explanation: The vulnerable window is exactly the execution duration, so slower operations are more likely to double-execute. This is why check-then-act fails precisely on the expensive operations you most wanted to protect.

L4.prompt_tpl: An idempotency record expires after {h} hours and a client retries with exponential backoff up to {d} hours after the original request. State the failure and the correct relationship between the two windows.
L4.answer: If the retry horizon exceeds the record lifetime, a late retry finds no record and re-executes, producing a duplicate charge long after the fact. The record window must strictly exceed the client's maximum retry horizon, including manual retries by support staff. h=24,d=48 and h=1,d=6 are broken; h=24,d=0.5 is safe. Document the window in the API so clients know when a key stops being honoured.
L4.explanation: Idempotency is only a property over a stated time window and the window is part of the contract. An unstated window means the client cannot know when a retry becomes a new request.

-- atomic token bucket in Redis, via Lua (KEYS[1] = bucket key)
  local b   = tonumber(ARGV[1])        -- burst capacity
  local r   = tonumber(ARGV[2])        -- refill per second
  local now = tonumber(ARGV[3])
  local t   = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
  local tokens = tonumber(t[1]) or b
  local ts     = tonumber(t[2]) or now
  tokens = math.min(b, tokens + (now - ts) * r)
  local ok = tokens >= 1
  if ok then tokens = tokens - 1 end
  redis.call('HMSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
  redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(b / r) * 2)
  return ok and 1 or 0
L0.cloze: The distributed limiter must be {{c1::atomic}}, which is why it runs as a {{c2::Lua}} script inside Redis rather than as a client-side read-modify-write. The key also needs an {{c3::EXPIRE}} so idle buckets do not accumulate forever.

concepts.L1: Token bucket for burst tolerance, sliding window log for accuracy, sliding window counter for a memory-accurate compromise. Distributed via Redis with Lua for atomicity.
concepts.L2: Fixed-window counters allow 2x the limit at a window boundary. Sliding window counter fixes it approximately with far less memory than a full log, and knowing that specific failure mode is a good detail.
concepts.L3: Fixed windows fail at boundaries by exactly a factor of two: a client sending its full limit $L$ in the last instant of one window and $L$ again in the first instant of the next has sent $2L$ within a span shorter than one window. The sliding window counter fixes it approximately by weighting the previous window's total by how much of it still lies inside the trailing window. Beyond the algorithm, three deployment details decide whether a limiter works: it must be atomic under concurrency, it must fail open or closed by explicit policy when Redis is down, and the response must carry limit, remaining and retry-after headers, or clients just retry blindly.

L4.prompt_tpl: A fixed-window limiter allows {L} requests per {w} seconds. Give the maximum a client can send within any single {w}-second span, and the instantaneous rate if both bursts land within {ms} ms of the boundary. Answer with the instantaneous rate in requests per second.
L4.answer: max in one window-length span $= 2L$; instantaneous rate $= 2L/(ms/1000)$ requests per second. L=100,ms=100: 200 requests in 0.1 s, 2000 rps. L=1000,ms=10: 2000 in 0.01 s, 200000 rps. The advertised rate was $L/w$, so at L=100,w=60 that is 1.67 rps.
L4.explanation: The boundary burst is not a small overshoot: it is a factor of two on the window and can be five orders of magnitude on the instant. Backends are sized for the instantaneous rate, which is why this failure mode causes real outages.

L4.prompt_tpl: Redis backing your rate limiter becomes unavailable while the service takes {q} requests per second. Choose fail-open or fail-closed and justify for an authentication endpoint and for a search endpoint.
L4.answer: Different answers per endpoint, which is the point. Authentication should fail closed or degrade to a strict local per-instance limit, because an unlimited authentication endpoint is a credential-stuffing opportunity and the security cost outweighs the availability cost. Search should fail open, because the limiter exists for capacity protection and taking search down to protect it inverts the goal; back it with a local in-process limiter as a coarse fallback.
L4.explanation: Fail-open versus fail-closed is a per-endpoint policy decision driven by whether the limiter is protecting capacity or protecting against abuse. A single global answer is wrong for one of the two.

     1 bit  unused (sign)
    41 bits milliseconds since a custom epoch   2^41 ms = 69.7 years
    10 bits machine id                          1024 machines
    12 bits sequence within the millisecond     4096 ids/ms/machine
    -> 4096 * 1000 = 4.096M ids/second/machine, 4.19e9 fleet-wide

  UUIDv7, 128 bits:
    48 bits unix milliseconds | 4 bits version | 12 bits rand_a
     2 bits variant | 62 bits rand_b
    -> time-ordered prefix, no coordination, standardised in RFC 9562
L0.cloze: Snowflake spends {{c1::41}} bits on milliseconds, {{c2::10}} on machine id and {{c3::12}} on a sequence, giving {{c4::4096}} ids per millisecond per machine. UUIDv7 puts {{c5::48}} bits of unix milliseconds in the high bits.

concepts.L1: Snowflake: timestamp, machine ID, sequence. Sortable by time, no coordination. UUIDv7 is the standardized modern version.
concepts.L2: Random UUIDv4 as a primary key destroys B-tree insert locality and causes page splits everywhere. UUIDv7's time prefix restores sequential insert behavior, and this is a real, measurable production issue.
concepts.L3: The insert-locality argument is measurable. A B-tree keyed on a random UUIDv4 scatters inserts uniformly across the key space, so every insert dirties a different leaf page; with a table larger than the buffer pool each insert becomes a read-modify-write of an uncached page, and page splits occur everywhere at once. A time-prefixed key concentrates inserts in the rightmost pages, which stay hot, so splits happen only at the boundary. The secondary effect is size: 16 bytes per UUID against 8 for a bigint, repeated in every secondary index, which on a billion-row table with four indexes is 32 GB of extra index. Snowflake's machine bits also need a lease service to allocate.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Snowflake variant uses {t} bits of milliseconds, {m} bits of machine id and {s} bits of sequence. Give the epoch lifetime in years, the machine count, and the maximum ids per second fleet-wide. Answer with the epoch lifetime in years.
L4.explanation: Every bit is a direct trade among lifetime, fleet size and burst rate within a millisecond. Sequence exhaustion within a millisecond forces the generator to spin until the clock advances, which is a real latency stall under burst.

L4.prompt_tpl: A table of {n} million rows with {idx} secondary indexes migrates its primary key from random UUIDv4 to UUIDv7. Give the index-size effect and the insert-locality effect, and say which one you would lead with.
L4.answer: Index size is unchanged: both are 16 bytes, so a switch from v4 to v7 saves nothing there, and only a move to a 64-bit id would. The effect is entirely locality: inserts move from scattered across the whole B-tree to concentrated in the rightmost pages, which turns each insert from a probable cache miss and page split into a hit on a hot page. Lead with locality, because it is the whole benefit.
L4.explanation: A common error is to attribute the UUIDv7 win to size. It is the same 128 bits; the ordering of those bits is the entire improvement, which is why the fix is a drop-in change with no schema migration.

concepts.L1: Inverted index, TF-IDF then BM25, sharding by document with scatter-gather, and hybrid dense-sparse retrieval for semantic search.
concepts.L2: Scatter-gather makes tail latency the dominant concern — you wait for the slowest shard. This is where tail latency amplification becomes concrete.
concepts.L3: TF-IDF is linear in term frequency, so a document repeating a term fifty times scores ten times one using it five times, which is wrong: the twentieth occurrence carries almost no additional evidence. BM25 saturates, approaching $k_{1}+1$ asymptotically, and its $b$ term divides by document length relative to the collection average so long documents are not favoured merely for having more words. On the systems side, sharding by document means every query touches every shard, so the fan-out tail arithmetic applies: at 16 shards and a per-shard p99 of 1 percent, 14.9 percent of queries are slow. The responses are partial results and hedging to a replica.

L4.prompt_tpl: A search index is sharded {S} ways with a per-shard slow probability of {p}, and every query is scatter-gather. Give the query slow probability, and the probability if the coordinator returns partial results once {frac} percent of shards have replied. Answer with the query slow probability when waiting for all shards.
L4.answer: waiting for all: $1-(1-p)^{S}$. S=16,p=0.01: 0.1485. S=64,p=0.01: 0.4746. S=128,p=0.005: 0.4735. With partial results at 90 percent of 64 shards, the query is slow only if more than 6 shards are slow simultaneously, which for $p = 0.01$ is a binomial tail of about $2 \times 10^{-7}$.

concepts.L2: Regulatory constraints often determine the architecture more than technical ones, and raising DPDP or GDPR unprompted in a design with user data reads as maturity.
